title: Building ServiceNow Apps with the Now SDK and Fluent (TypeScript, Source-Control-First)
excerpt: ServiceNow now ships a code-first way to build apps: define tables, business rules, script includes and ACLs as TypeScript using Fluent, then build and install from your own machine. A practical tour grounded in the official sdk-examples repo.
content:
Two ways to build on ServiceNow

For years, building an application on ServiceNow meant clicking through the platform UI — Studio, App Engine Studio, the form designer — and letting the instance store every artifact as a record. That still works. But ServiceNow now ships a second, complementary path: the Now SDK (also called the ServiceNow SDK), where you describe your application as TypeScript source files on your own machine using a declarative library called Fluent, then build and deploy it to an instance.

This article is a practical, code-first tour of that workflow, grounded in the official ServiceNow/sdk-examples repository, the Australia-family Fluent docs, and npx @servicenow/sdk explain (CLI docs for Fluent APIs).

The one-line summary: Fluent lets you define tables, business rules, script includes, ACLs, REST APIs and more as version-controlled code, so a ServiceNow app can live in Git and be built in a normal CI pipeline — like any other software project.

Why a code-first SDK exists

  • Real source control. Update Sets and even scoped-app Git integration are record-centric. With the SDK, your app is the source tree — clean diffs, pull requests, and code review work the way engineers expect.
  • Local development. Author in VS Code with TypeScript types, autocomplete, and your own linters and formatters. No round-trip to the instance to write a Business Rule.
  • Repeatable builds. A build step turns your TypeScript into deployable metadata, so the same commit produces the same app on dev, test, and prod.
  • It complements Studio — it does not replace it. You can still open the app in the platform; the SDK simply gives a code path for teams that want one.

Prerequisites

  • Node.js v20+ and a package manager (the samples use pnpm; npm works too).
  • The SDK packages: @servicenow/sdk, @servicenow/glide (server-side type definitions), and typescript.
  • Access to a ServiceNow instance where you can authenticate and deploy a scoped application.

Anatomy of an SDK project

Every SDK app is a normal Node project. The pieces that matter:

my-app/
  now.config.json          // app scope + build config
  package.json             // deps + the "now-sdk build" script
  src/
    fluent/                // your Fluent (*.now.ts) declarations
      index.now.ts
      generated/keys.ts    // auto-generated stable IDs (do not hand-edit)
    server/                // server-side .js used by rules/script includes

The now.config.json pins the application scope so builds are deterministic:

{
  "scope": "x_myapp",
  "scopeId": "fc1b5713c3db3110d6489a038a40dd84",
  "serverModulesDir": "src/server"
}

And package.json wires up the build command:

{
  "name": "my-app",
  "scripts": {
    "build": "now-sdk build"
  },
  "devDependencies": {
    "@servicenow/sdk": "latest",
    "@servicenow/glide": "latest",
    "typescript": "latest"
  }
}

Fluent by example

Fluent gives you a typed function for each platform artifact. You import it from @servicenow/sdk/core, call it with a configuration object, and the build turns that into the corresponding record(s) in your scoped app. The magic identifier Now.ID['...'] assigns a stable, generated key so re-deploys update the same record instead of creating duplicates.

1. A table

import { DateTimeColumn, IntegerColumn, StringColumn, Table } from '@servicenow/sdk/core'

export const x_myapp_order = Table({
    name: 'x_myapp_order',
    label: 'Order',
    schema: {
        order_number: StringColumn({ label: 'Order Number', mandatory: true }),
        quantity: IntegerColumn({ label: 'Quantity', mandatory: true }),
        ordered_at: DateTimeColumn({ label: 'Ordered At' }),
    },
})

2. A Business Rule

JavaScript modules are the modern, preferred approach for server-side logic in Fluent projects (typed Glide APIs via @servicenow/glide, import/export, reuse). Now.include() still inlines a file at build time when you want a classic script field.

import { BusinessRule } from '@servicenow/sdk/core'
import { setOrderPriority } from '../server/set-order-priority'

BusinessRule({
    $id: Now.ID['set_order_priority'],
    name: 'Set Order Priority',
    active: true,
    table: 'x_myapp_order',
    when: 'before',
    action: ['insert', 'update'],
    script: setOrderPriority,
})

The module under src/server/ is ordinary ServiceNow server JavaScript — the same GlideRecord / gs APIs you already know — with optional TypeScript types from @servicenow/glide.

3. A Script Include

import { ScriptInclude } from '@servicenow/sdk/core'

ScriptInclude({
    $id: Now.ID['order-utils'],
    name: 'OrderUtils',
    active: true,
    apiName: 'x_myapp.OrderUtils',
    script: Now.include('./OrderUtils.server.js'),
})

4. An ACL

Security is code too. Roles and record ACLs are declared alongside everything else, so access control ships and reviews with the feature it protects:

import { Acl, Role } from '@servicenow/sdk/core'

export const orderManager = Role({ name: 'x_myapp.order_manager' })

Acl({
    $id: Now.ID['order_write_acl'],
    type: 'record',
    operation: 'write',
    table: 'x_myapp_order',
    roles: [orderManager],
})
The sdk-examples repo has focused samples for each of these — plus Scripted REST APIs, UI Actions, Script Actions, Flows, ATF tests, cross-scope modules, and React / Svelte / Vue / SolidJS UI pages. Cloning it and running pnpm install is the fastest way to see real, buildable Fluent.

Build and deploy

The everyday loop is small:

# scaffold a new app (interactive, or use --appName/--scopeName flags)
npx @servicenow/sdk init

# type-check + transform Fluent into deployable metadata
npx @servicenow/sdk build

# authenticate, then install the built app on the instance
# (CLI alias: now-sdk deploy → now-sdk install)
npx @servicenow/sdk auth --add <instance-url> --type basic
npx @servicenow/sdk install

Because the output is deterministic, the same command runs in CI: install dependencies, now-sdk build, run your ATF tests, then deploy to the target instance. That is the whole point — a ServiceNow app that behaves like any other codebase.

SDK / Fluent vs App Engine Studio — when to use which

Use the Now SDK + Fluent when…Use App Engine Studio / UI when…
The team is engineering-led and wants Git, PRs, and code reviewCitizen developers or admins are building quickly in-platform
You need repeatable CI/CD builds across environmentsA single instance, low change velocity, Update Sets are enough
You want TypeScript types, local linting, and diff-able sourceYou prefer guided, low-code form and flow designers
The app is large, long-lived, and shared across a teamThe app is small or experimental

They are not mutually exclusive: an app built with the SDK still opens in the platform, and you can adopt the SDK for the parts of an app that benefit most from source control.

Gotchas worth knowing

  • Do not hand-edit generated/keys.ts. Those stable IDs are what let re-deploys update existing records instead of duplicating them.
  • Prefer server modules; classic scripts still follow platform rules. Fluent is modern TypeScript, but server modules and inlined scripts still run under the platform engine — keep scoped-vs-global scripting rules in mind. Never invent sys_ids; always use Now.ID['key'].
  • Scope is fixed by now.config.json. Changing scope after records exist is disruptive; decide the scope up front.
  • The SDK evolves quickly. Pin your @servicenow/sdk version and check the release notes before upgrading — argument shapes and available components expand release over release.

Where to go next

  • ServiceNow/sdk-examples — official, buildable samples for every component type.
  • ServiceNow SDK (Australia docs) — CLI, Fluent, and install workflow.
  • npx @servicenow/sdk explain <topic> — local Fluent API reference (BusinessRule, Table, Acl, Flow, …).

If you already know GlideRecord and scoped apps, the SDK is not a new platform to learn — it is a cleaner front door to the one you already use.

title: AI Agents in ServiceNow: What They Are, How They Work, and When to Use Them (Beginner Guide)
excerpt: AI Agents go beyond chatbots and assistants — they can reason, plan, and take multi-step actions autonomously. This guide explains what they are, how they differ from Virtual Agent and Now Assist, and the practical path to deploying them.
content:
What Are AI Agents?

AI Agents in ServiceNow are autonomous AI workers that can reason about a task, plan the steps needed, execute those steps, and handle errors — all without a human telling them what to do at each stage.

This is fundamentally different from the other AI capabilities in ServiceNow:

Now AssistVirtual AgentAI Agents
RoleAssistant — suggests and draftsChatbot — follows scripted flowsWorker — reasons and acts autonomously
Decision makingHuman makes the decision, AI provides informationPre-built decision trees — bot follows the programmed pathAI makes decisions within defined boundaries
Autonomy levelLow — always advisoryMedium — follows rules but can branchHigh — plans and executes multi-step tasks
When human is involvedAlways — human reviews every suggestionOnly on escalation (handoff to live agent)Only for exceptions outside the agent's scope or confidence

The Everyday Analogy

Think about the difference between these three workplace roles:

  • Now Assist = a research assistant. You ask them to summarize a report or draft an email. They do the work, but you review and send it yourself.
  • Virtual Agent = a receptionist with a script. They greet visitors, answer common questions from a FAQ, and direct people to the right department. They follow a defined process.
  • AI Agent = a junior analyst who can work independently. You give them a task ("handle this incoming request"), and they figure out the steps: check the request type, look up policies, verify eligibility, create the necessary records, notify the right people, and close the loop. They come to you only when they encounter something outside their training.

How AI Agents Work — The Reasoning Loop

An AI Agent follows a reasoning loop that is fundamentally different from a scripted workflow:

Trigger: New P1 incident created with no assignment group
        ↓
AI Agent receives the task:
  "Investigate and route this P1 incident"
        ↓
REASONING STEP 1: "What kind of incident is this?"
  → Agent reads the short description, category, and affected CI
  → Agent uses Knowledge Graph to find similar past incidents
  → Conclusion: "This is a database connectivity issue on the payment server"
        ↓
REASONING STEP 2: "Who should handle this?"
  → Agent looks up the CI's support group in the CMDB
  → Agent checks the on-call schedule for that group
  → Conclusion: "Database Operations team, Jane Doe is on-call"
        ↓
REASONING STEP 3: "What else needs to happen for a P1?"
  → Agent checks P1 procedures: bridge call required, exec notification required
  → Agent creates a bridge call task
  → Agent sends executive notification
        ↓
ACTION: Agent updates the incident:
  - Assignment group: Database Operations
  - Assigned to: Jane Doe
  - Work notes: "AI Agent analysis: Database connectivity issue on payment
    server CM0001234. Similar to INC0045678 (resolved by restarting
    connection pool). Routed to Database Operations per CMDB ownership.
    Bridge call created. Executive notification sent."
        ↓
MONITORING: Agent monitors for resolution
  → If not acknowledged in 15 min → escalate to backup
  → If resolved → generate resolution summary

Notice the difference from a workflow: a workflow would need every possible path pre-programmed. The AI Agent reasons about the situation and decides what to do based on the context.

AI Agent Studio — Where You Build Agents

AI Agent Studio is the visual builder for creating and configuring AI Agents.

// Navigate to: All > AI Agent Studio
//
// When building an agent, you define:
//
// 1. PURPOSE — What is this agent responsible for?
//    Example: "Route and enrich incoming P1 incidents"
//
// 2. TOOLS — What actions can the agent take?
//    - Look Up Record (read CMDB, incident history, KB)
//    - Update Record (set fields on the incident)
//    - Create Record (create tasks, notifications)
//    - Knowledge Graph search
//    - Call Subflow (trigger a Flow Designer automation)
//    - File Upload / Download
//    - Send Notification
//
// 3. GUARDRAILS — What can the agent NOT do?
//    - Cannot delete records
//    - Cannot change priority (only a human can de-escalate a P1)
//    - Cannot access HR data tables
//    - Must explain its reasoning in work notes
//
// 4. ESCALATION — When should the agent hand off to a human?
//    - Confidence below 60% on intent classification
//    - No similar past incidents found
//    - Customer is VIP with special handling rules
//    - Agent has taken 5+ actions without resolution

Tools — What AI Agents Can Do

AI Agents are given access to tools — specific capabilities they can use during execution. The agent decides which tools to use based on the situation.

ToolWhat It DoesExample Use
Look Up RecordQuery any ServiceNow tableLook up the affected CI's support group, check the caller's VIP status, find similar past incidents
Update RecordModify fields on existing recordsSet assignment group, update priority, add work notes
Create RecordCreate new records in any tableCreate a child task, create a change request, create a problem record
Knowledge GraphSearch connected knowledge across CMDB, KB, and service relationshipsFind which business service is affected, find the owner, find relevant KB articles
Call SubflowExecute a Flow Designer subflowTrigger a password reset, create a bridge call, send a Slack notification
Predictive IntelligenceRun ML models for classificationPredict the correct category, assignment group, and priority

AI Agents in Virtual Agent

One of the most powerful combinations: an AI Agent running inside a Virtual Agent conversation. Instead of following rigid scripted topic flows, the Virtual Agent hands off to an AI Agent that can reason about the user's request in real time.

// Traditional Virtual Agent:
//   User says "my laptop is slow"
//   Bot follows scripted flow: "Have you restarted?" → Yes/No → ...
//   Every possible path must be pre-built
//
// Virtual Agent + AI Agent:
//   User says "my laptop is slow"
//   AI Agent reasons: check user's device in CMDB → check recent incidents
//   for that device → check if there's a known issue →
//   "I see your laptop was imaged 3 years ago and has 4GB RAM.
//    There's a hardware refresh program available. Would you like me
//    to submit a replacement request?"
//
// The AI Agent handles the conversation dynamically based on data,
// not a pre-scripted decision tree.

When to Use What — The Decision Framework

ScenarioUse ThisWhy
User needs to check ticket statusVirtual Agent (scripted topic)Simple lookup — no reasoning needed, just a GlideRecord query
Agent needs a ticket summaryNow Assist skillAdvisory — agent reviews and uses the summary
Password reset requestVirtual Agent + Flow DesignerWell-defined process with clear steps — scripted flow is sufficient
Route a P1 incident with CMDB contextAI AgentRequires reasoning about CI relationships, team availability, and P1 procedures
Handle a complex, multi-step employee onboardingAI AgentMany conditional steps, cross-department coordination, exceptions handling
Generate resolution notes at ticket closeNow Assist skillSingle-task AI assistance, human reviews output
Automatically resolve known-error incidentsAI Agent + Predictive IntelligenceAI matches to known error, applies fix, verifies, closes — fully autonomous

Governance and Safety

Because AI Agents can take actions autonomously, governance is critical:

ControlWhat It Prevents
Tool restrictionsAgent can only use tools you explicitly grant. No tool = no access.
Table/field ACLsStandard ServiceNow ACLs apply. The AI Agent runs under a service account with specific roles — it cannot access tables or fields its role does not permit.
Confidence thresholdsIf the agent's confidence in its reasoning drops below a threshold, it escalates to a human instead of guessing.
Action limitsMaximum number of actions per execution. Prevents runaway loops.
Human-in-the-loopFor high-impact actions (delete, major field changes), require human approval before the agent acts.
Audit loggingEvery action the AI Agent takes is logged — what it reasoned, what tools it used, what changes it made. Full audit trail.
AI Control TowerDashboard showing all AI Agent activity across the instance — usage, errors, escalations, compliance status.

The Adoption Path — How to Get There

AI Agents are not a day-one deployment. They require a mature foundation:

  1. Phase 1: Data Foundation — Clean CMDB, structured KB, consistent categorization. Without good data, AI Agents make bad decisions.
  2. Phase 2: Now Assist — Deploy AI assistance for agents. Prove AI value with lower-risk advisory capabilities.
  3. Phase 3: Virtual Agent — Deploy scripted self-service chatbot. Learn which use cases work well and which need human judgment.
  4. Phase 4: Predictive Intelligence — Deploy ML-based categorization and routing. Build confidence in AI-driven decisions.
  5. Phase 5: AI Agents (Pilot) — Pick one well-defined, high-volume use case (e.g., known-error auto-resolution). Build the agent with strict guardrails. Monitor closely.
  6. Phase 6: AI Agents (Expand) — Expand to more use cases as confidence and governance maturity grow.

The #1 Mistake

Deploying AI Agents before the data foundation is solid. An AI Agent that routes incidents based on bad CMDB data will misroute them at scale — faster than a human would, and without the judgment to realize something is wrong. Fix your data first, then automate.

title: Virtual Agent from Zero: The Beginner-Friendly Guide to ServiceNow's Conversational AI
excerpt: Everything you need to understand Virtual Agent — what it is, how it works, the components you configure, and how it connects to Now Assist and AI Agents. Written for people who have never built a chatbot before.
content:
What is Virtual Agent?

Virtual Agent is ServiceNow's conversational chatbot — it lets employees interact with ServiceNow by typing (or speaking) in natural language instead of filling out forms. Think of it as the text-based equivalent of calling a help desk, but available 24/7 and capable of resolving many common requests instantly.

The Simplest Way to Understand It

Imagine an employee at your company needs to reset their password at 11 PM on a Saturday. Without Virtual Agent, they either wait until Monday or call an expensive after-hours support line. With Virtual Agent:

  1. Employee opens the ServiceNow portal or Teams/Slack
  2. Types: "I need to reset my password"
  3. Virtual Agent recognizes the intent ("password reset")
  4. Bot asks: "Which system? (Active Directory, SAP, Salesforce)"
  5. Employee selects "Active Directory"
  6. Bot verifies identity (security questions or MFA)
  7. Bot triggers an automated password reset workflow
  8. Employee gets a new temporary password in under 2 minutes
  9. No human agent was involved. No ticket was created.

Where Virtual Agent Appears

ChannelHow Users Access It
Service PortalChat widget in the bottom-right corner of the ServiceNow portal
Employee CenterIntegrated into the modern employee experience portal
Microsoft TeamsUsers chat with the ServiceNow bot directly in Teams — no need to open a browser
SlackSame as Teams — chat with the bot in Slack channels or DMs
Now MobileChat within the ServiceNow mobile app
Web APICustom integrations can send messages to Virtual Agent programmatically

Key Components of Virtual Agent

Virtual Agent is built from several components that work together:

1. Topics

A topic is a single conversation flow for one specific task. "Reset password," "Check ticket status," "Request a laptop" — each is a separate topic. Think of each topic as a mini-program: it has a trigger (what the user says), a conversation flow (what the bot asks and does), and an outcome (resolution or escalation).

2. NLU (Natural Language Understanding)

NLU is what makes Virtual Agent understand what the user means, not just what they typed. When a user says "my password doesn't work," "can't log in," or "locked out of my account" — NLU maps all of these to the same intent: password reset.

ConceptWhat It IsExample
IntentWhat the user wants to do"Reset password," "Check order status," "Report an issue"
UtterancesThe different ways users express the same intent"I forgot my password," "can't log in," "password expired," "locked out"
EntitiesSpecific data within the user's messageSystem name ("Active Directory"), location ("Building A"), device type ("laptop")
Confidence ScoreHow sure the AI is about its interpretation (0-100%)Above 80% → proceed with the matched topic. Below 50% → ask user to clarify.

3. Topic Blocks

Within a topic, the conversation is built from blocks — each block is one step in the conversation:

Block TypeWhat It DoesExample
TextBot sends a message to the user"I can help you reset your password."
User InputBot asks the user for information"Which system do you need the password reset for?"
ChoiceBot presents options for the user to selectButtons: [Active Directory] [SAP] [Salesforce]
DecisionBot branches based on a conditionIf system = "Active Directory" → go to AD reset flow; else → go to generic flow
ScriptExecute server-side JavaScriptLook up the user's account status, check if they have MFA enabled
Flow / SubflowTrigger a Flow Designer flowTrigger the "Reset Active Directory Password" subflow
Create RecordCreate a ServiceNow recordCreate an incident or request if the bot cannot resolve the issue
Agent TransferEscalate to a live agent"I am connecting you with a live agent who can help further."

4. Live Agent Handoff

Not every conversation can be resolved by the bot. When the bot cannot handle a request — either the confidence is too low, the topic is too complex, or the user explicitly asks for a human — Virtual Agent transfers the chat to a live agent in Agent Workspace. The agent sees the full conversation transcript so the user does not have to repeat themselves.

Virtual Agent + Now Assist + AI Agents: How They Connect

These three AI capabilities are related but serve different purposes:

Virtual AgentNow AssistAI Agents
What it isConversational chatbot for usersAI assistant for agents and creatorsAutonomous AI workers that execute tasks
Who it helpsEnd users / employeesSupport agents, developers, adminsThe system itself (reduces human involvement)
How it worksUser chats → bot understands intent → follows topic flow → resolves or escalatesAgent opens ticket → AI summarizes, suggests, drafts → agent reviews and actsTrigger fires → AI Agent reasons about steps → executes actions → updates record
Level of autonomyGuided (follows pre-built topic flows)Assistive (suggests, human decides)Autonomous (AI decides and acts within guardrails)
ExampleUser asks "reset my password" → bot resets itAgent clicks "Summarize" → AI generates summary → agent uses itP1 incident created → AI Agent identifies root cause, routes to team, sends notification — no human triggered these steps

How they work together: A user chats with Virtual Agent (front door). If the bot cannot resolve, it creates a ticket and escalates to a live agent. The live agent uses Now Assist (AI suggestions, summaries) to resolve faster. For routine patterns that happen thousands of times, AI Agents can handle the entire process autonomously — from the initial chat to the final resolution — with no human involvement.

Building Your First Topic — Step by Step

// Navigate to: All > Virtual Agent > Topic Conversation Design
// Click "New" to create a topic
//
// 1. SETUP
//    Name: "Reset Password"
//    Category: IT Support
//    NLU Intent: password_reset (link to your NLU model)
//    Sample utterances: "I forgot my password", "can't log in",
//                       "locked out", "password expired", "reset pwd"
//
// 2. BUILD THE CONVERSATION FLOW
//    Block 1: Text — "I can help you reset your password."
//    Block 2: Choice — "Which system?"
//             Options: Active Directory, SAP, Salesforce, Other
//    Block 3: Decision — If "Active Directory" → go to Block 4
//                        If "Other" → go to Agent Transfer
//    Block 4: Script — Verify user identity (check user record, MFA status)
//    Block 5: Subflow — Trigger "Reset AD Password" Flow Designer subflow
//    Block 6: Text — "Your password has been reset. Your temporary
//                     password has been sent to your email."
//    Block 7: End conversation
//
// 3. TEST
//    Use the "Try it" panel on the right side of the designer
//    Type "I can't log in" and verify the bot follows the correct path
//
// 4. PUBLISH
//    Set topic to "Published" to make it live
//    Monitor in Virtual Agent Analytics

Common Virtual Agent Use Cases

Use CaseEstimated DeflectionComplexity
Password reset70-90%Medium (requires integration with AD/LDAP)
Check ticket status80-95%Low (simple GlideRecord lookup)
Request software access60-80%Medium (catalog item + approval workflow)
VPN troubleshooting40-60%Medium (decision tree based on symptoms)
Report an incident50-70%Low-Medium (create incident with pre-filled fields)
HR policy questions60-80%Low (KB article search and presentation)
Order equipment70-85%Medium (catalog item submission)

Measuring Virtual Agent Success

MetricWhat It MeasuresHealthy Target
Containment RatePercentage of conversations resolved without live agentAbove 60% for mature implementations
Deflection RateTickets avoided because Virtual Agent resolved the issue20-40% of eligible categories
User SatisfactionEnd-of-conversation survey ratingAbove 4.0/5.0
NLU AccuracyPercentage of intents correctly identifiedAbove 80% confidence on matched intents
Escalation RateHow often conversations escalate to live agentsBelow 40% — high escalation means topics need improvement

title: Now Assist Skills Deep Dive: Every Skill, Every Module, and How to Set Them Up
excerpt: The complete reference for every Now Assist skill across ITSM, HRSD, CSM, and Creator — what each skill does, which plugin activates it, where it appears in the UI, and the step-by-step setup in the Admin Console.
content:
What This Article Covers

Now Assist is organized into skills — individual AI capabilities grouped by product module. Each skill can be independently enabled, configured, and monitored. This article is the complete reference: every skill, what it does, which plugin powers it, where it appears in the UI, and how to set it up.

The Now Assist Admin Console — Your Control Center

Before diving into individual skills, you need to know where everything is managed.

// Access the Admin Console:
// Navigate to: All > Now Assist > Now Assist Admin
//
// What you see:
// ┌─────────────────────────────────────┐
// │  Dashboard                           │ → Usage stats, active skills, model health
// │  Skills                              │ → Enable/disable/configure individual skills
// │  Settings                            │ → Plugins, LLM config, data sharing
// │  Analytics                           │ → Acceptance rates, feedback, trends
// │  Generative AI Controller            │ → Guardrails, PII rules, topic restrictions
// └─────────────────────────────────────┘

ITSM Skills (IT Service Management)

Install: the Now Assist for ITSM application (ServiceNow Store / Application Manager)

These skills are designed for IT support agents who handle incidents, problems, and changes.

Incident Summarization

What it does: Reads the entire history of an incident — work notes, additional comments, activity log, state transitions, and related records — and generates a concise human-readable summary.

Where you see it: The Now Assist panel on the right side of the incident form in Agent Workspace. Agent clicks "Summarize" and the summary appears within seconds.

When it is most valuable: Complex incidents with dozens of comments spanning days or weeks. Escalated incidents where the new agent needs context fast. Shift handoffs where the incoming agent needs to catch up on all active P1s.

Data dependency: Quality depends entirely on work note quality. If agents write detailed, structured notes, summaries are excellent. If work notes are empty or say "called user, waiting," the summary will reflect that emptiness.

Resolution Notes Generation

What it does: When an agent resolves an incident, this skill drafts the close notes based on the work notes, actions taken, and resolution approach. The agent reviews the draft, edits if needed, and saves.

Where you see it: The Resolution Information section when the agent changes state to Resolved.

Why it matters: Consistent, complete resolution notes are critical for knowledge management and trend analysis. Most agents write minimal close notes when pressed for time. AI-generated drafts ensure every ticket has useful closure documentation.

Chat Summarization

What it does: Summarizes a live chat or Virtual Agent conversation transcript. Particularly valuable when a chat gets transferred from Virtual Agent to a live agent, or from one agent to another.

Where you see it: Agent Workspace chat panel.

Chat Reply Recommendation

What it does: During a live chat, suggests a response for the agent based on the conversation context and knowledge base content. The agent can accept the suggestion, modify it, or ignore it.

Where you see it: Below the chat input field — "Suggested reply" text that the agent can click to insert.

Data dependency: Quality depends on knowledge base coverage. If there are good KB articles for the topic being discussed, recommendations are strong. If the KB is sparse, recommendations will be generic.

KB Article Generation

What it does: After resolving an incident, drafts a knowledge base article from the incident details and resolution. The idea: if this incident was resolved, the solution should be captured so the next person with the same issue can self-serve.

Where you see it: Post-resolution action — a "Create KB Article" option that generates a draft article.

Change Request Summarization

What it does: Summarizes complex change requests — particularly useful for CAB (Change Advisory Board) reviewers who need to understand the change, its risk, and its impact without reading every detail.

Sidebar Discussion Summarization

What it does: Summarizes sidebar chat discussions (collaboration chats) that occurred during incident resolution, so team members joining later can catch up.

HRSD Skills (HR Service Delivery)

Install: the Now Assist for HRSD application (ServiceNow Store / Application Manager)

Same core capabilities as ITSM but tailored for HR workflows. Key difference: HR data is more sensitive (PII, compensation, health), so guardrail configuration is critical.

HR Case Summarization

Same concept as Incident Summarization but for HR cases — benefits disputes, accommodation requests, employee relations issues.

Resolution Notes Generation

Drafts closure documentation for HR cases.

Chat Summarization & Reply Recommendation

Supports HR chat interactions — particularly important for live agent handoffs during sensitive conversations.

KB Article Generation

Generates HR knowledge articles from resolved cases — "How to update tax withholding," "Steps to request FMLA leave."

Privacy Note

HR data often contains PII and sensitive information. Before enabling HRSD skills, configure the Generative AI Controller to ensure PII is properly handled — names, SSNs, salary information, and health data should be filtered from AI prompts where appropriate.

CSM Skills (Customer Service Management)

Install: the Now Assist for CSM application (ServiceNow Store / Application Manager)

Designed for customer-facing support teams.

Customer Case Summarization

Summarizes customer support cases — essential when cases span multiple agents, channels (chat, email, phone), and weeks of back-and-forth.

Email Reply Recommendation

Unique to CSM: Drafts email responses to customer inquiries. The AI considers the case history, product context, and KB articles to generate a professional, contextual reply. The agent reviews and sends.

Voice Call Summarization

Unique to CSM: When phone calls are transcribed, this skill summarizes the transcript into key points, action items, and next steps.

Chat Reply Recommendation & Chat Summarization

Same as ITSM equivalents but configured for customer-facing conversations — tone and language are adjusted for external communication.

Creator Skills (For Developers and Admins)

Install: the Now Assist for Creator application (ServiceNow Store / Application Manager)

These skills help people build on the platform faster.

Flow Generation

What it does: Describe a flow in natural language ("create a flow that sends a Slack notification when a P1 incident is created and the assignment group is empty") and AI generates the Flow Designer configuration.

Where you see it: Flow Designer — natural language input field.

Code Assist (Intelligent Code Recommendations)

What it does: AI-powered code completion in the ServiceNow script editor. Suggests the next lines of code, explains existing scripts, and generates GlideRecord queries from descriptions.

Where you see it: Script editor across the platform — Business Rules, Script Includes, Client Scripts, etc.

Catalog Item Generation

What it does: Describe a catalog item and AI generates the item configuration including variables, workflow, and approval rules.

Playbook Generation & Recommendation

What it does: Generates process playbook steps from descriptions and recommends playbook templates based on the use case.

App Generation

What it does: Generates a starter application structure from a plain-English description of what the app should do.

Data Visualization Generation

What it does: Creates dashboards and report visualizations from natural language — "show me P1 incidents by assignment group over the last 6 months as a line chart."

The Skill Kit — Building Custom Skills

When the out-of-box skills do not cover your use case, the Now Assist Skill Kit lets you build custom skills. This is an intermediate-to-advanced capability.

// What you can do with the Skill Kit:
//
// 1. Define a custom prompt template
//    - System instructions + data context + user request
//    - Example: "Summarize this change request focusing on risk factors"
//
// 2. Connect custom data sources
//    - Pull from any ServiceNow table (not just OOB ones)
//    - Include related record data, custom fields, attachments
//
// 3. Deploy to Now Assist panel or Context Menu
//    - Appears alongside OOB skills in the Agent Workspace
//    - Or as a right-click option on text fields (Elaborate, Shorten, Analyze)
//
// 4. Use Automated Prompt Optimization (APO)
//    - Feed a dataset of 100+ records
//    - APO reviews skill performance and suggests prompt improvements
//    - Measures: correctness, faithfulness, latency
//
// 5. Integrate Predictive Intelligence
//    - Add ML classification models to custom skills
//    - Combine generative AI (text) with predictive AI (classification)

LLM Configuration — Which Model Powers It

OptionWhat It IsWhen to Use It
Now LLMServiceNow's own hosted LLM. Data stays within ServiceNow boundary.Default choice for most deployments. Best for data sovereignty and compliance.
Azure OpenAIMicrosoft-hosted OpenAI models connected via API.When your organization already has Azure OpenAI contracts or needs specific model capabilities.
CustomBring-your-own LLM endpoint.Advanced scenarios where neither Now LLM nor Azure OpenAI meets requirements.
// Configure LLM settings in:
// Now Assist Admin Console > Settings > LLM Configuration
//
// Key settings:
// - Active model (Now LLM or Azure OpenAI)
// - API endpoint and credentials (for Azure OpenAI)
// - Token limits per request
// - Fallback behavior if primary model is unavailable

Guardrails and Governance

Before enabling skills at scale, configure the Generative AI Controller:

// Navigate to: Now Assist Admin > Generative AI Controller
//
// Key configurations:
// 1. PII Handling
//    - Mask PII in prompts (names, emails, SSNs, phone numbers)
//    - Configure which PII types to mask vs. allow
//
// 2. Topic Restrictions
//    - Block AI from generating content on certain topics
//    - E.g., "Do not generate content about legal advice"
//
// 3. Response Quality
//    - Max response length
//    - Required citation of source data
//    - Confidence threshold (below which AI declines to answer)
//
// 4. Audit Logging
//    - Every AI interaction logged
//    - What was sent to the model, what came back
//    - Who requested it, when, and what action they took (accept/edit/dismiss)

Implementation Advice

Start with one module (ITSM is usually the best first choice — highest volume, most mature data). Enable 2-3 skills for a pilot group. Measure acceptance rates and feedback for 4-6 weeks. Then expand to more skills and more modules. The phased approach consistently outperforms big-bang AI rollouts.

title: CSDM End to End: How a Single Outage Traces from a Linux Box to a Business Service (With Tables, Queries, and the Stuff Nobody Explains)
excerpt: Walk through CSDM the way it actually works in production. One outage, traced from infrastructure CI through application service to business service to the executive who gets the call. Every table, every relationship, every query.
content:
What this article is

I have set up CSDM in multiple enterprise instances and the one thing I can tell you is — the official documentation gives you a model diagram and a list of tables, but nobody walks you through what actually happens when a server goes down at 2 AM and someone needs to know which business service just broke.

This article does that. One scenario, end to end. Every layer of CSDM, every table involved, every relationship that matters, and the GlideRecord queries to prove it.

The scenario

Your company runs an online ordering system. Customers place orders on the website, the order goes through a payment gateway, hits an order processing API, writes to a database, and triggers a fulfillment workflow. All of this runs on a handful of Linux servers in AWS.

At 2:14 AM on a Tuesday, one of the database servers runs out of disk space. The order processing API starts throwing 500 errors. Within minutes, the website checkout page is broken. Customers cannot complete purchases.

Here is the question CSDM answers: how does the on-call engineer — and then the VP of Commerce — know that a full disk on server DB-PROD-03 means the "Online Ordering" business service is down?

The layers — bottom to top

CSDM is not one flat table. It is a stack of layers, each representing a different level of abstraction. The official model has 7 domains now (CSDM 5.0), but for understanding the core service chain, you need to internalize these layers:

LayerWhat it representsTableExample in our scenario
Infrastructure CIsPhysical or virtual compute, storage, networkcmdb_ci_server, cmdb_ci_linux_server, cmdb_ci_databaseDB-PROD-03 (Linux server), OrderDB (MySQL instance)
ApplicationA discoverable running software instancecmdb_ci_applOrder Processing API (Node.js app running on APP-PROD-01)
Service Instance / Application ServiceA logical grouping of applications and infra that delivers a specific technical capabilitycmdb_ci_service_auto"Order Processing Service" — the API + database + message queue working together
Business ApplicationA logical, governed representation of a software system in the portfoliocmdb_ci_business_app"Online Ordering Platform" — the application as leadership knows it
Business ServiceA service published to the business, visible to users and executivescmdb_ci_service_business"Online Ordering" — the thing the VP of Commerce talks about in quarterly reviews
Business Service OfferingA specific flavor or tier of a business service with SLA commitmentsservice_offering"Online Ordering - Production" (99.9% SLA) vs "Online Ordering - Staging" (best effort)

The relationships — how they connect

The layers above are useless without relationships between them. This is where most CSDM implementations fail. Teams populate the tables but never build the connections.

ServiceNow stores CI relationships in the cmdb_rel_ci table. Each row says "CI A is related to CI B with relationship type X."

// The relationship chain for our scenario:
//
// DB-PROD-03 (cmdb_ci_linux_server)
//    |
//    | "Hosts" relationship
//    v
// OrderDB (cmdb_ci_database)
//    |
//    | "Used By" relationship
//    v
// Order Processing API (cmdb_ci_appl)
//    |
//    | "Members Of::Contains" relationship
//    v
// Order Processing Service (cmdb_ci_service_auto)   <-- Application Service
//    |
//    | "Depends On::Used By" relationship
//    v
// Online Ordering Platform (cmdb_ci_business_app)
//    |
//    | "Managed By::Manages" relationship
//    v
// Online Ordering (cmdb_ci_service_business)        <-- Business Service
//    |
//    | related via service_offering table
//    v
// Online Ordering - Production (service_offering)   <-- with SLA commitments

Without these relationships, when DB-PROD-03 fills up, the incident just says "server disk full." Nobody knows it affects ordering. With CSDM relationships, the impact chain is visible immediately — and automated.

Setting it up — the practical steps

Step 1: Create the Business Service

Start from the top. The business service is what executives care about. You do not start with servers.

// Navigate to: cmdb_ci_service_business.list
// Create new record:
//   Name: Online Ordering
//   Owned by: VP of Commerce (sys_user reference)
//   Support group: E-Commerce Operations (sys_user_group)
//   Operational status: Operational
//   Install status: Installed
//   Business criticality: 1 - Most Critical

// Or via script:
var bs = new GlideRecord('cmdb_ci_service_business');
bs.initialize();
bs.name = 'Online Ordering';
bs.owned_by = 'sys_id_of_vp_commerce';
bs.support_group = 'sys_id_of_ecom_ops_group';
bs.operational_status = 1;  // Operational
bs.install_status = 1;      // Installed
bs.busines_criticality = 1; // Most Critical
bs.insert();

Step 2: Create the Business Application

// Navigate to: cmdb_ci_business_app.list
// Create new record:
//   Name: Online Ordering Platform
//   Owned by: Engineering Manager
//   Managed by business service: Online Ordering
//   SDLC lifecycle stage: Production

var ba = new GlideRecord('cmdb_ci_business_app');
ba.initialize();
ba.name = 'Online Ordering Platform';
ba.owned_by = 'sys_id_of_eng_manager';
ba.install_status = 1;
ba.insert();

Step 3: Create the Application Service (Service Instance)

This is the operational grouping. It represents the deployed technical stack that delivers a capability.

// Navigate to: cmdb_ci_service_auto.list
// Create new record:
//   Name: Order Processing Service
//   Owned by: Lead SRE
//   Managed by application: Online Ordering Platform
//   Environment: Production

var as = new GlideRecord('cmdb_ci_service_auto');
as.initialize();
as.name = 'Order Processing Service';
as.owned_by = 'sys_id_of_lead_sre';
as.install_status = 1;
as.insert();

Step 4: Build the relationships

This is the part that makes CSDM actually work. Without relationships, you just have disconnected records.

// Create relationship: Application Service -> Business Application
// "Depends On::Used By"
var rel = new GlideRecord('cmdb_rel_ci');
rel.initialize();
rel.parent = ba.sys_id;   // Business Application (upstream)
rel.child = as.sys_id;    // Application Service (downstream)
rel.type = 'sys_id_of_depends_on_used_by_rel_type';
// Look up relationship type sys_id:
// var rt = new GlideRecord('cmdb_rel_type');
// rt.addQuery('name', 'Depends on::Used by');
// rt.query(); rt.next(); // rt.sys_id is what you need
rel.insert();

// Create relationship: Business Service -> Business Application
var rel2 = new GlideRecord('cmdb_rel_ci');
rel2.initialize();
rel2.parent = bs.sys_id;  // Business Service
rel2.child = ba.sys_id;   // Business Application
rel2.type = 'sys_id_of_manages_managed_by_rel_type';
rel2.insert();

// Infrastructure CIs (servers, databases) are typically
// populated by Discovery, not manually. Discovery scans your
// network, finds running services, and creates the CIs
// and their relationships automatically.

The 2 AM outage — how CSDM makes it visible

Now the disk fills up on DB-PROD-03. An event fires. An incident is created. Here is what happens with CSDM in place versus without it.

Without CSDM

// Incident created:
//   Short description: Disk space critical on DB-PROD-03
//   CI: DB-PROD-03
//   Priority: calculated from impact/urgency, but nobody knows
//             what this server actually affects
//   Assignment group: Linux Admins
//
// The Linux admin sees a disk full alert. Cleans up temp files.
// Meanwhile, orders are failing for 45 minutes.
// The VP finds out from a customer tweet, not from ServiceNow.

With CSDM

// Incident created:
//   Short description: Disk space critical on DB-PROD-03
//   CI: DB-PROD-03
//   
// ServiceNow automatically traces the impact:
//   DB-PROD-03 hosts OrderDB
//   OrderDB is used by Order Processing API
//   Order Processing API is part of Order Processing Service
//   Order Processing Service supports Online Ordering Platform
//   Online Ordering Platform is managed by "Online Ordering" business service
//   "Online Ordering" is Business Criticality: 1 - Most Critical
//
// Incident auto-escalated to P1.
// Assignment group: E-Commerce Operations (from business service support group)
// VP of Commerce gets an automatic notification.
// SLA clock starts ticking on the 99.9% commitment.

Querying the impact chain

Here is the script that walks the relationship chain from a CI to its business service. This is what happens under the hood during impact analysis.

// Given a CI sys_id (e.g., the failing database server),
// find all business services impacted.

function getImpactedBusinessServices(ciSysId) {
    var visited = {};
    var businessServices = [];

    function walkUp(sysId, depth) {
        if (visited[sysId] || depth > 10) return;
        visited[sysId] = true;

        // Check if this CI is itself a business service
        var check = new GlideRecord('cmdb_ci_service_business');
        if (check.get(sysId)) {
            businessServices.push({
                name: check.getValue('name'),
                owner: check.getDisplayValue('owned_by'),
                criticality: check.getDisplayValue('busines_criticality')
            });
            return;
        }

        // Find upstream CIs (parents in relationships)
        var rel = new GlideRecord('cmdb_rel_ci');
        rel.addQuery('child', sysId);
        rel.query();
        while (rel.next()) {
            walkUp(rel.getValue('parent'), depth + 1);
        }
    }

    walkUp(ciSysId, 0);
    return businessServices;
}

// Usage:
var impacted = getImpactedBusinessServices('sys_id_of_db_prod_03');
impacted.forEach(function(svc) {
    gs.info('IMPACTED: ' + svc.name + ' | Owner: ' + svc.owner +
            ' | Criticality: ' + svc.criticality);
});
// Output: IMPACTED: Online Ordering | Owner: VP Commerce | Criticality: 1 - Most Critical

CSDM 5.0 — what changed and what you actually need to know

The model went from 5 domains in 4.0 to 7 domains in 5.0. Most of the additions are about strategic planning and AI, not about the core service chain. Here is what matters practically:

What changedOld nameNew name / additionWhy it matters
Application Service renamedApplication ServiceService Instance (Application Service is now a subtype)Other service types added: Data Service, Network Service, etc. Your existing Application Services still work — just reclassified.
Technical Service renamedTechnical ServiceTechnology Management ServiceJust a label change. Same table, same function.
New: Ideation & Strategy domainDid not existProduct Ideas, Strategic Priorities, Goals, TargetsConnects strategic planning to service delivery. Matters for SPM users, not for day-to-day ITSM.
New: AI Data ModelDid not existdm_ai_system_digital_asset, AI Function, AI ApplicationIf you are deploying Now Assist or AI agents, these CIs track your AI components in the CMDB.
New: SBOMDid not existSoftware Bill of MaterialsTracks software component dependencies. Critical for SecOps vulnerability scanning.
New: Value StreamsDid not existValue Stream entity in Foundation domainMaps how work flows to deliver value. Connects to Process Mining.

For most teams doing ITSM, the core chain (Infrastructure → Application Service → Business Application → Business Service) has not changed. CSDM 5.0 is additive — it does not break your existing model.

The adoption path — Crawl, Walk, Run, Fly

ServiceNow recommends a phased approach. I have seen teams try to jump to "Run" and it always fails. Here is what each phase actually means in practice:

PhaseWhat you doWhat you get
FoundationClean up locations, departments, groups, users. Get your org structure right. Define lifecycle statuses.Basic data hygiene. Nothing CSDM-specific yet, but without this the rest falls apart.
CrawlCreate Business Services and Business Applications. Assign owners. Map them to each other.Portfolio visibility. Executives can see which apps support which services. No infra mapping yet.
WalkCreate Application Services. Connect them to infrastructure CIs via Discovery. Build the full relationship chain.Impact analysis works. Incidents on a CI can trace to business services. Change risk assessment uses service context.
RunService Mapping validates relationships continuously. CMDB Health tracks completeness. Lifecycle management enforced.Trusted, maintained CMDB. Automation depends on it. Now Assist uses it for context. AI agents query it.
FlyFull CSDM 5.0 with Value Streams, SBOM, AI models, strategic alignment.Enterprise-wide service intelligence. Not many organizations are here yet.

Where teams get it wrong

I have watched enough CSDM implementations to know the patterns that kill them:

  • Starting with infrastructure. Teams spend 6 months loading servers into CMDB and never get to business services. Start from the top. Business services first, then work down.
  • No ownership. Every Business Application and Business Service needs an owner. If the owned_by field is empty, nobody is accountable. Nobody maintains the data. It rots.
  • Missing relationships. 500 CIs with zero relationships is a flat spreadsheet, not CSDM. The value is in the connections between layers. Run this query regularly:
// Find business applications with no relationships at all
var ba = new GlideRecord('cmdb_ci_business_app');
ba.addQuery('install_status', 1);  // Installed
ba.query();
while (ba.next()) {
    var rel = new GlideRecord('cmdb_rel_ci');
    rel.addQuery('parent', ba.sys_id);
    rel.addOrCondition('child', ba.sys_id);
    rel.setLimit(1);
    rel.query();
    if (!rel.next()) {
        gs.info('ORPHAN: ' + ba.getValue('name') + ' has zero relationships');
    }
}
  • Using custom tables instead of CSDM tables. I have seen teams create u_my_services instead of using cmdb_ci_service_business. Then Service Mapping does not work. Impact analysis does not work. Every ServiceNow product that reads service data expects the CSDM tables. Use them.
  • Treating CSDM as a one-time project. It is not. Services change, apps get retired, new infrastructure spins up. You need ongoing governance — Discovery schedules, Health Dashboard monitoring, ownership reviews. Set up a recurring monthly check or it degrades within a quarter.

The health check query

Run this to get a quick read on your CSDM maturity:

// CSDM Health Check - run in Background Scripts
var tables = [
    {name: 'cmdb_ci_service_business', label: 'Business Services'},
    {name: 'cmdb_ci_business_app', label: 'Business Applications'},
    {name: 'cmdb_ci_service_auto', label: 'Application Services (Service Instances)'},
    {name: 'service_offering', label: 'Service Offerings'}
];

tables.forEach(function(t) {
    var gr = new GlideRecord(t.name);
    gr.addQuery('install_status', 1);
    gr.query();
    var total = gr.getRowCount();

    // Count those without owners
    var noOwner = new GlideAggregate(t.name);
    noOwner.addQuery('install_status', 1);
    noOwner.addNullQuery('owned_by');
    noOwner.addAggregate('COUNT');
    noOwner.query();
    var unowned = noOwner.next() ? parseInt(noOwner.getAggregate('COUNT')) : 0;

    gs.info(t.label + ': ' + total + ' total, ' + unowned + ' without owner (' +
            (total > 0 ? Math.round(unowned/total*100) : 0) + '% unowned)');
});

// Check relationship coverage
var bs = new GlideAggregate('cmdb_ci_service_business');
bs.addQuery('install_status', 1);
bs.addAggregate('COUNT');
bs.query();
var totalBS = bs.next() ? parseInt(bs.getAggregate('COUNT')) : 0;

var withRel = 0;
var bsGr = new GlideRecord('cmdb_ci_service_business');
bsGr.addQuery('install_status', 1);
bsGr.query();
while (bsGr.next()) {
    var rel = new GlideRecord('cmdb_rel_ci');
    rel.addQuery('parent', bsGr.sys_id);
    rel.addOrCondition('child', bsGr.sys_id);
    rel.setLimit(1);
    rel.query();
    if (rel.next()) withRel++;
}
gs.info('Business Services with at least one relationship: ' +
        withRel + '/' + totalBS + ' (' +
        (totalBS > 0 ? Math.round(withRel/totalBS*100) : 0) + '%)');

How this connects to interview questions

If an interviewer asks you about CSDM, they are not looking for you to recite the 7 domains. They want to hear:

  • That you understand why CSDM exists — connecting technical failures to business impact
  • That you know the actual table names — cmdb_ci_service_business, cmdb_ci_business_app, cmdb_ci_service_auto, cmdb_rel_ci
  • That you can describe a real scenario where CSDM changes the outcome — like the 2 AM outage above
  • That you know the adoption path is phased, not big-bang — Foundation, Crawl, Walk, Run
  • That you have an opinion on where teams fail — no ownership, no relationships, custom tables instead of OOB

That combination — table knowledge, scenario thinking, and implementation experience — is what separates someone who read a blog post from someone who has actually done it.

title: Conditions and Query Building in ServiceNow: Filters, Encoded Queries, Condition Builder, and Script Equivalents
excerpt: Every way to filter records in ServiceNow — from the UI condition builder to encoded queries to GlideRecord addQuery to dot-walking. How they connect and when to use each one.
content:
Three ways to filter records

In ServiceNow, you filter records in three places. They all generate the same thing underneath — an encoded query.

WhereHowUsed by
List filter (UI)Condition builder — dropdown menusAdmins, end users
Encoded query stringText string like priority=1^active=trueURL params, scripts, reports
GlideRecord addQueryJavaScript method callsDevelopers in scripts

The condition builder (UI)

Every list view has a filter icon (funnel). Click it, and you get the condition builder. You pick a field, an operator, and a value. You can chain conditions with AND/OR.

After building your filter, you can get the encoded query string: right-click the breadcrumb above the list and select "Copy query". This gives you a string you can paste into scripts.

Encoded query syntax

An encoded query is a string representation of filter conditions. ^ means AND. ^OR means OR. ^NQ means a new query (OR group).

// Simple conditions
priority=1                          // priority equals 1
active=true                         // active is true
state!=6                            // state is not 6 (Resolved)

// Chaining with AND (^)
priority=1^active=true^state!=6
// priority = 1 AND active = true AND state != 6

// OR conditions (^OR)
priority=1^ORpriority=2
// priority = 1 OR priority = 2

// Grouped OR with AND
priority=1^ORpriority=2^active=true
// (priority = 1 OR priority = 2) AND active = true

// Special operators
short_descriptionLIKEvpn           // contains 'vpn'
short_descriptionSTARTSWITHEmail   // starts with 'Email'
short_descriptionENDSWITHfailed    // ends with 'failed'
assigned_toISEMPTY                 // field is empty
assigned_toISNOTEMPTY              // field is not empty
sys_created_on>2026-01-01        // created after Jan 1
sys_created_onONToday              // created today
sys_created_onRELATIVEGE@hour@ago@24  // created in last 24 hours

// Reference field dot-walking
assignment_group.name=Network Ops   // group name (through reference)
caller_id.department.name=IT        // caller's department name

// IN operator
stateIN1,2,3                       // state is 1, 2, or 3
stateNOT IN6,7                     // state is not 6 or 7

Using encoded queries in scripts

// Instead of multiple addQuery calls:
var gr = new GlideRecord('incident');
gr.addQuery('priority', 1);
gr.addQuery('active', true);
gr.addQuery('state', '!=', 6);
gr.query();

// You can do this in one line:
var gr = new GlideRecord('incident');
gr.addEncodedQuery('priority=1^active=true^state!=6');
gr.query();

// Both produce the exact same SQL query. Use whichever is clearer.
// For complex filters, encoded queries are often easier to read
// and you can copy them directly from the list filter UI.

Building encoded queries dynamically

// Build a query string from variables
var table = 'incident';
var maxAge = 30;
var groups = ['Network Ops', 'Database Admins'];

var query = 'active=true';
query += '^sys_created_on>=' + gs.daysAgo(maxAge);
query += '^assignment_group.nameIN' + groups.join(',');

var gr = new GlideRecord(table);
gr.addEncodedQuery(query);
gr.query();
gs.info('Matching records: ' + gr.getRowCount());

Dot-walking

Dot-walking lets you traverse reference fields to access fields on related records. It works in queries, getValue, and getDisplayValue.

var gr = new GlideRecord('incident');
gr.addQuery('priority', 1);
gr.query();
while (gr.next()) {
    // Direct field
    gs.info(gr.getValue('number'));

    // One level: caller's name
    gs.info(gr.getDisplayValue('caller_id'));

    // Two levels: caller's department name
    gs.info(gr.getValue('caller_id.department'));       // sys_id of department
    gs.info(gr.getDisplayValue('caller_id.department')); // 'IT'

    // Three levels: caller's department head's email
    gs.info(gr.getValue('caller_id.department.dept_head.email'));
}

// Dot-walking in queries works the same way:
var gr = new GlideRecord('incident');
gr.addQuery('caller_id.department.name', 'IT');
gr.addQuery('caller_id.vip', true);
gr.query();
// Finds incidents where the caller is in the IT department AND is a VIP

Dot-walking performance trap

// BAD: dot-walking inside a loop fires a separate query per row
var gr = new GlideRecord('incident');
gr.addQuery('active', true);
gr.setLimit(500);
gr.query();
while (gr.next()) {
    // Each of these is a separate database query!
    var email = gr.caller_id.email.toString();
    var dept = gr.caller_id.department.name.toString();
}
// For 500 rows, this could be 1000+ extra queries.

// BETTER: query the related table separately and build a lookup
var users = {};
var userGr = new GlideRecord('sys_user');
userGr.addQuery('sys_id', 'IN', callerIds.join(','));
userGr.query();
while (userGr.next()) {
    users[userGr.getValue('sys_id')] = {
        email: userGr.getValue('email'),
        dept: userGr.getDisplayValue('department')
    };
}

Condition builder in Business Rules, Notifications, etc.

Many ServiceNow configuration records (Business Rules, Notifications, UI Policies, ACLs) have a "Condition" field that uses the same condition builder as list filters. The condition is stored as an encoded query string internally.

// When you configure a Business Rule with condition:
//   priority = 1 AND state changes to Resolved
// The platform stores it as:
//   priority=1^stateVALCHANGES6

// VALCHANGES is a special operator meaning "value changed to"
// It only evaluates to true during the transaction where the change happens.
// Other special operators:
//   VALCHANGES  — value changed to
//   ANYTHING    — field was modified (any change)
//   SAMEAS      — same as another field's value
//   NSAMEAS     — not same as another field's value

Quick reference table

I want toUI operatorEncoded queryaddQuery equivalent
Equalsispriority=1addQuery('priority', 1)
Not equalsis notstate!=6addQuery('state', '!=', 6)
Greater thangreater thanpriority>2addQuery('priority', '>', 2)
Containscontainsshort_descriptionLIKEvpnaddQuery('short_description', 'CONTAINS', 'vpn')
Starts withstarts withnumberSTARTSWITHINCaddQuery('number', 'STARTSWITH', 'INC')
Is emptyis emptyassigned_toISEMPTYaddNullQuery('assigned_to') or encoded assigned_toISEMPTY
In listis one ofstateIN1,2,3addQuery('state', 'IN', '1,2,3')
Changed tochanges tostateVALCHANGES6current.state.changesTo(6) (in BR)

title: Every Scripting Keyword That Matters in ServiceNow: current, previous, g_form, gs, and the Objects You Must Know
excerpt: The built-in objects and keywords injected into every script context. What they are, what they contain, when they are null, and the mistakes that come from not understanding them.
content:
How ServiceNow injects objects into your scripts

When you write a Business Rule, Client Script, or Script Include, ServiceNow wraps your code and injects specific objects depending on the context. You do not import or declare these — they just exist.

current (server-side)

Available in: Business Rules, Workflow scripts, Flow Designer script steps

current is a GlideRecord object pointing to the record being operated on. When a user saves an incident, current is that incident.

// Before Business Rule on incident table
(function executeRule(current, previous) {
    gs.info(current.getValue('number'));        // INC0010001
    gs.info(current.getValue('state'));          // 1
    gs.info(current.getTableName());             // incident
    gs.info(current.isNewRecord());              // true on insert, false on update
    gs.info(current.isActionAborted());          // false (unless someone called setAbortAction)

    // Modify the record before it saves
    current.priority = 1;
    current.work_notes = 'Auto-escalated by Business Rule';

    // Abort the save entirely
    // current.setAbortAction(true);
    // gs.addErrorMessage('Cannot save: missing required data');
})(current, previous);

When current is null

  • Script Includes called directly (not from a BR context) — current is not defined
  • Background Scripts — current is not defined unless you create your own GlideRecord
  • Scheduled Jobs — current is not defined

previous (server-side)

Available in: Business Rules (update and delete operations only)

previous is a read-only GlideRecord snapshot of the record BEFORE the current changes. It lets you compare old vs new values.

(function executeRule(current, previous) {
    // Check if priority changed
    if (current.getValue('priority') != previous.getValue('priority')) {
        gs.info('Priority changed from ' + previous.getValue('priority') +
                ' to ' + current.getValue('priority'));
    }

    // Check if the record was reassigned
    if (current.getValue('assigned_to') != previous.getValue('assigned_to')) {
        gs.info('Reassigned from ' + previous.getDisplayValue('assigned_to') +
                ' to ' + current.getDisplayValue('assigned_to'));
    }
})(current, previous);

When previous is null

  • On insert: previous is null — there is no "before" state for a new record. Always check: if (previous) before using it.
  • In async Business Rules: previous is NOT available. Async BRs run outside the original transaction, so the previous state is gone.
  • In Display Business Rules: previous is not available (the record is being read, not modified).
// Safe pattern — always guard against null previous
(function executeRule(current, previous) {
    if (previous && current.state.changesTo(6)) {
        // State changed to Resolved — only runs on update, not insert
        gs.eventQueue('incident.resolved', current, gs.getUserID(), '');
    }
})(current, previous);

GlideElement methods on current/previous

When you access current.priority, you do not get a number or string. You get a GlideElement object with these methods:

// changes() — did this field change in this transaction?
if (current.priority.changes()) {
    gs.info('Priority was modified');
}

// changesTo(value) — did it change TO this specific value?
if (current.state.changesTo(6)) {
    gs.info('State just changed to Resolved');
}
// NOTE: the value must be the INTERNAL value (number), not the display label.
// changesTo('Resolved') will NOT work. Use changesTo(6).

// changesFrom(value) — did it change FROM this specific value?
if (current.state.changesFrom(1)) {
    gs.info('Was previously New, now something else');
}

// nil() — is the field empty/null?
if (current.assigned_to.nil()) {
    gs.info('Nobody assigned');
}

// toString() — convert GlideElement to string
var desc = current.short_description.toString();

// getDisplayValue() — the human-readable label
gs.info(current.state.getDisplayValue());  // 'New', 'In Progress', etc.

// getReferenceTable() — for reference fields, get the target table
gs.info(current.caller_id.getReferenceTable());  // 'sys_user'

// getRefRecord() — get the full referenced record
var callerGR = current.caller_id.getRefRecord();
gs.info(callerGR.getValue('email'));  // caller's email address

gs (GlideSystem) — the utility belt

Available in: all server-side scripts. gs is a global object with system utility methods.

User context

gs.getUserID();           // sys_id of logged-in user
gs.getUserName();         // 'john.smith'
gs.getUserDisplayName();  // 'John Smith'
gs.hasRole('admin');      // true/false
gs.hasRole('itil');       // true/false

// Get the full user GlideRecord
var userGR = gs.getUser().getRecord();
gs.info(userGR.getValue('email'));

Messages

// These show banners on the user's screen (only in before/after BRs)
gs.addInfoMessage('Record updated successfully.');
gs.addErrorMessage('Cannot save: priority 1 requires an assignment group.');

// These do NOT work in:
// - Async Business Rules (user's transaction is already done)
// - Scheduled Jobs (no user session)
// - Script Includes called from REST APIs

Dates and time

gs.now();                    // '2026-04-07 14:30:00' (user's timezone)
gs.nowDateTime();            // '2026-04-07 14:30:00' (system format)
gs.daysAgo(7);               // date/time 7 days ago
gs.daysAgoStart(7);          // start of day, 7 days ago (midnight)
gs.beginningOfLastMonth();   // first day of previous month
gs.endOfLastMonth();         // last day of previous month

Checking for empty values

// gs.nil() is the safest way to check for empty values
gs.nil(null);       // true
gs.nil(undefined);  // true
gs.nil('');         // true
gs.nil(0);          // false (zero is not nil)
gs.nil('hello');    // false

// Use it to guard against empty fields
var assignee = gr.getValue('assigned_to');
if (gs.nil(assignee)) {
    gs.info('No assignee');
}

g_form (client-side)

Available in: Client Scripts, UI Actions (client-side). NOT available on the server.

g_form controls the form the user is looking at in their browser.

// onChange Client Script
function onChange(control, oldValue, newValue, isLoading) {
    if (isLoading) return;  // do not run when the form first loads

    // Read a field value
    var priority = g_form.getValue('priority');  // '1', '2', '3', etc.

    // Set a field value
    g_form.setValue('urgency', '1');

    // Make a field mandatory
    g_form.setMandatory('assignment_group', true);

    // Hide a field
    g_form.setVisible('u_internal_only', false);

    // Show a message
    g_form.addInfoMessage('Priority updated.');
}

// onLoad Client Script — runs when the form opens
function onLoad() {
    if (g_form.isNewRecord()) {
        g_form.setValue('contact_type', 'self-service');
    }
}

// onSubmit Client Script — runs when the user clicks Save
function onSubmit() {
    var desc = g_form.getValue('short_description');
    if (desc.length < 10) {
        g_form.addErrorMessage('Description must be at least 10 characters.');
        return false;  // prevents the form from submitting
    }
    return true;
}

g_user (client-side)

// Available in Client Scripts
g_user.userName;          // 'john.smith'
g_user.userID;            // sys_id of current user
g_user.getFullName();     // 'John Smith'
g_user.hasRole('itil');   // true/false
g_user.hasRoleExactly('incident_manager');  // true only for that specific role

// Common pattern: show/hide fields based on role
function onLoad() {
    if (!g_user.hasRole('itil')) {
        g_form.setVisible('u_technical_notes', false);
    }
}

The client-server boundary

This is the single most important concept in ServiceNow scripting. The server and client are completely separate environments. You cannot call GlideRecord from a Client Script. You cannot call g_form from a Business Rule.

Getting server data from the client: GlideAjax

// Step 1: Create a Script Include on the server
// Name: IncidentUtils
// Must extend AbstractAjaxProcessor to be callable from client
var IncidentUtils = Class.create();
IncidentUtils.prototype = Object.extendsObject(AbstractAjaxProcessor, {
    getCallerEmail: function() {
        var userId = this.getParameter('sysparm_user_id');
        var gr = new GlideRecord('sys_user');
        if (gr.get(userId)) {
            return gr.getValue('email');
        }
        return '';
    },
    type: 'IncidentUtils'
});

// Step 2: Call it from a Client Script
function onChange(control, oldValue, newValue, isLoading) {
    if (isLoading || !newValue) return;

    var ga = new GlideAjax('IncidentUtils');
    ga.addParam('sysparm_name', 'getCallerEmail');
    ga.addParam('sysparm_user_id', newValue);
    ga.getXMLAnswer(function(answer) {
        // 'answer' is the string returned by the server method
        g_form.setValue('u_caller_email', answer);
    });
}

// KEY RULES:
// 1. Script Include MUST extend AbstractAjaxProcessor
// 2. Use this.getParameter() to read params on the server
// 3. Always use getXMLAnswer with a callback (async)
// 4. Return values are always strings

Pushing server data to the client: g_scratchpad

// Display Business Rule (server-side, runs on form load)
(function executeRule(current, previous) {
    g_scratchpad.isVIP = String(current.caller_id.vip == true);
    g_scratchpad.openCount = '42';  // must be string/simple types
})(current, previous);

// Client Script (onLoad) — reads g_scratchpad
function onLoad() {
    if (g_scratchpad.isVIP === 'true') {
        g_form.addInfoMessage('This caller is a VIP.');
    }
}
// g_scratchpad avoids a GlideAjax round-trip.
// Use it for data you know you will need on every form load.

Putting it all together: a real example

// GOAL: When a user sets priority to 1 on an incident form,
// make assignment_group mandatory, show a warning,
// and auto-populate the escalation contact from the server.

// === Before Business Rule (server) ===
// Table: incident, When: before, Insert/Update: true
(function executeRule(current, previous) {
    if (current.getValue('priority') == '1' && current.assigned_to.nil()) {
        // Server-side validation — catches API and import submissions too
        current.setAbortAction(true);
        gs.addErrorMessage('P1 incidents must have an assigned person.');
    }
})(current, previous);

// === Client Script (onChange on priority field) ===
function onChange(control, oldValue, newValue, isLoading) {
    if (isLoading) return;
    if (newValue == '1') {
        g_form.setMandatory('assignment_group', true);
        g_form.addInfoMessage('P1 selected — assignment group is now required.');

        // Fetch escalation contact from server
        var ga = new GlideAjax('IncidentUtils');
        ga.addParam('sysparm_name', 'getEscalationContact');
        ga.addParam('sysparm_group', g_form.getValue('assignment_group'));
        ga.getXMLAnswer(function(contact) {
            if (contact) {
                g_form.setValue('u_escalation_contact', contact);
            }
        });
    } else {
        g_form.setMandatory('assignment_group', false);
    }
}

// This covers both sides: the client makes the field mandatory
// and shows a message, while the server enforces it for API callers
// who bypass the form entirely.

title: JavaScript Inside ServiceNow: var, let, const, Types, and What Actually Runs Where
excerpt: ServiceNow runs JavaScript but it is not the same JavaScript you write in a browser or Node.js. This is the ground-up reference — variables, types, scope, and the engine differences that trip people up from day one.
content:
The first thing to know

ServiceNow runs two completely separate JavaScript environments. Code that works on one side will crash on the other.

Server-sideClient-side
Runs inServiceNow's Java-based server (Rhino engine)The user's web browser
Script typesBusiness Rules, Script Includes, Scheduled Jobs, Fix Scripts, Background ScriptsClient Scripts, UI Policies (scripted), UI Actions (client)
JS versionES5 (no let/const, no arrow functions, no template literals in global scope)Modern ES6+ (depends on the user's browser)
Database accessYes — GlideRecord, GlideAggregateNo — must use GlideAjax to call server
Available objectscurrent, previous, gs, GlideRecordg_form, g_user, g_list

Variables: var, let, const

Server-side (Business Rules, Script Includes)

The server uses the Rhino engine which only supports ES5 in global scope. That means:

// This works everywhere on the server:
var name = 'incident';
var count = 0;
var isActive = true;

// This FAILS in global-scope server scripts:
// let name = 'incident';    // SyntaxError
// const MAX = 100;          // SyntaxError
// var msg = `Hello ${name}`; // SyntaxError — no template literals

// EXCEPTION: Scoped applications run on a newer engine (ES2021+)
// In scoped apps, let/const/arrow functions DO work:
// let x = 10;  // works in scoped app scripts
// const y = 20; // works in scoped app scripts

Rule of thumb: In global scope, use var. In scoped applications, you can use let and const. When in doubt, use var — it works everywhere.

Client-side (Client Scripts)

Client scripts run in the browser, so modern JS works fine:

// All of these work in Client Scripts:
var oldWay = 'works';
let newWay = 'also works';
const CONSTANT = 'works too';
var msg = `Hello ${oldWay}`; // template literals work

var vs let — the actual difference

// var is function-scoped — it leaks out of blocks
for (var i = 0; i < 5; i++) {
    // i is visible here
}
gs.info(i); // 5 — var leaks out of the for loop

// let is block-scoped — it stays inside the block
for (let j = 0; j < 5; j++) {
    // j is visible here
}
// gs.info(j); // ReferenceError — j does not exist here

// const — like let but cannot be reassigned
const MAX_RETRIES = 3;
// MAX_RETRIES = 5; // TypeError — cannot reassign

Data types

// String
var desc = 'Server is down';
var desc2 = "Also a string";  // single or double quotes both work

// Number (integer and decimal are the same type)
var priority = 1;
var percent = 99.5;

// Boolean
var isActive = true;
var isClosed = false;

// Null and Undefined
var assigned = null;       // explicitly set to nothing
var notSet;                // undefined — never assigned a value
// gs.nil() checks for null, undefined, AND empty string:
gs.info(gs.nil(null));       // true
gs.info(gs.nil(undefined));  // true
gs.info(gs.nil(''));         // true
gs.info(gs.nil('hello'));    // false

// Array
var priorities = [1, 2, 3, 4];
gs.info(priorities[0]);     // 1
gs.info(priorities.length); // 4

// Object
var config = {
    table: 'incident',
    limit: 50,
    active: true
};
gs.info(config.table);      // 'incident'
gs.info(config['limit']);   // 50 — bracket notation also works

Type gotchas in ServiceNow

GlideRecord fields do not return plain JavaScript types. They return GlideElement objects. This causes bugs that are hard to spot.

var gr = new GlideRecord('incident');
gr.get('number', 'INC0010001');

// WRONG — comparing a GlideElement to a string
if (gr.priority == '1') {
    // This MIGHT work, but it is unreliable.
    // gr.priority is a GlideElement object, not a string.
}

// CORRECT — use getValue() to get the raw string value
if (gr.getValue('priority') == '1') {
    // This always works. getValue returns a plain string.
}

// WRONG — concatenating GlideElement into a string
var msg = 'Priority is ' + gr.priority;
// This calls toString() on the GlideElement, which usually works
// but can behave unexpectedly with reference fields.

// CORRECT — explicit getValue
var msg = 'Priority is ' + gr.getValue('priority');

// WRONG — storing a GlideElement in a variable for later use
var saved = gr.caller_id;
gr.next(); // moves to next record
gs.info(saved); // NOW POINTS TO THE NEW RECORD'S caller_id!
// GlideElement is a reference to the cursor position, not a copy.

// CORRECT — store the value, not the element
var saved = gr.getValue('caller_id');
gr.next();
gs.info(saved); // still has the original value

Functions

// Basic function (works everywhere)
function calculatePriority(impact, urgency) {
    if (impact == 1 && urgency == 1) return 1;
    if (impact == 1 || urgency == 1) return 2;
    return 3;
}
var p = calculatePriority(1, 2); // returns 2

// Function in a Business Rule (the wrapper pattern)
// ServiceNow wraps your BR code in an IIFE:
(function executeRule(current, previous) {
    // 'current' = the record being saved
    // 'previous' = the record before changes (null on insert)

    current.priority = calculatePriority(
        current.getValue('impact'),
        current.getValue('urgency')
    );
})(current, previous);

// Arrow functions — ONLY in scoped apps or client scripts
// var calc = (a, b) => a + b;  // fails in global server scope
// Use regular functions on the server in global scope.

Loops

// for loop — iterate a known number of times
for (var i = 0; i < 10; i++) {
    gs.info('Iteration ' + i);
}

// while loop — the GlideRecord pattern
var gr = new GlideRecord('incident');
gr.addQuery('active', true);
gr.setLimit(100);
gr.query();
while (gr.next()) {
    gs.info(gr.getValue('number'));
}
// gr.next() returns false when there are no more records

// for...in — iterate over object keys
var config = { table: 'incident', limit: 50 };
for (var key in config) {
    gs.info(key + ' = ' + config[key]);
}
// Output: table = incident, limit = 50

// Array iteration
var items = ['one', 'two', 'three'];
for (var i = 0; i < items.length; i++) {
    gs.info(items[i]);
}
// .forEach works in scoped apps and client scripts:
// items.forEach(function(item) { gs.info(item); });

Conditionals

// if / else if / else
var priority = gr.getValue('priority');
if (priority == '1') {
    gs.info('Critical');
} else if (priority == '2') {
    gs.info('High');
} else {
    gs.info('Normal or lower');
}

// == vs === (loose vs strict equality)
gs.info(1 == '1');   // true — loose comparison, converts types
gs.info(1 === '1');  // false — strict comparison, different types
