// In ServiceNow, getValue() always returns strings, so:
// gr.getValue('priority') == 1   → true (loose, works)
// gr.getValue('priority') === 1  → false (strict, different types)
// gr.getValue('priority') === '1' → true (strict, both strings)
// Best practice: use == when comparing getValue output to numbers,
// or convert explicitly: Number(gr.getValue('priority')) === 1

// Ternary operator
var label = (priority == '1') ? 'Critical' : 'Not critical';

// Switch statement
switch (gr.getValue('state')) {
    case '1': gs.info('New'); break;
    case '2': gs.info('In Progress'); break;
    case '6': gs.info('Resolved'); break;
    case '7': gs.info('Closed'); break;
    default: gs.info('Other state');
}

Strings

var desc = 'Email server down in building A';

desc.length;                    // 33
desc.indexOf('server');         // 6 (position of first match)
desc.indexOf('xyz');            // -1 (not found)
desc.includes('server');        // true (scoped apps/client only)
desc.toLowerCase();             // 'email server down in building a'
desc.toUpperCase();             // 'EMAIL SERVER DOWN IN BUILDING A'
desc.substring(0, 5);          // 'Email'
desc.split(' ');                // ['Email', 'server', 'down', 'in', 'building', 'A']
desc.replace('down', 'offline'); // 'Email server offline in building A'
desc.trim();                    // removes leading/trailing whitespace

// String concatenation
var msg = 'Incident ' + gr.getValue('number') + ' is priority ' + gr.getValue('priority');

// Template literals (scoped apps and client scripts only)
// var msg = `Incident ${number} is priority ${priority}`;

Arrays

var groups = ['Network', 'Database', 'Security'];

groups.length;          // 3
groups[0];              // 'Network'
groups.push('Storage'); // adds to end: ['Network','Database','Security','Storage']
groups.pop();           // removes last: ['Network','Database','Security']
groups.indexOf('Database'); // 1
groups.join(', ');      // 'Network, Database, Security'

// Check if value exists in array
if (groups.indexOf('Network') !== -1) {
    gs.info('Found it');
}

// Build an array from GlideRecord results
var numbers = [];
var gr = new GlideRecord('incident');
gr.addQuery('priority', 1);
gr.setLimit(10);
gr.query();
while (gr.next()) {
    numbers.push(gr.getValue('number'));
}
gs.info('P1 incidents: ' + numbers.join(', '));

Objects / JSON

// Create an object
var incident = {
    number: 'INC0010001',
    priority: 1,
    active: true,
    tags: ['network', 'vpn']
};

// Access properties
gs.info(incident.number);       // 'INC0010001'
gs.info(incident['priority']);  // 1

// Add/modify properties
incident.state = 'New';
incident.priority = 2;

// Convert to JSON string (for logging, REST payloads, etc.)
var jsonStr = JSON.stringify(incident);
gs.info(jsonStr);
// {"number":"INC0010001","priority":2,"active":true,"tags":["network","vpn"],"state":"New"}

// Parse JSON string back to object
var parsed = JSON.parse(jsonStr);
gs.info(parsed.number); // 'INC0010001'

// Common use: REST API responses
var response = new sn_ws.RESTMessageV2('MyAPI', 'GET');
var body = response.execute().getBody();
var data = JSON.parse(body);  // parse response body into usable object

Error handling

// try/catch — prevent your script from crashing the entire transaction
try {
    var gr = new GlideRecord('incident');
    gr.get('number', 'INC0010001');
    var result = JSON.parse(gr.getValue('u_custom_json_field'));
    gs.info(result.key);
} catch (e) {
    gs.error('Failed to parse JSON: ' + e.message);
    // The script continues instead of crashing
}

// try/catch/finally
try {
    // risky operation
} catch (e) {
    gs.error('Error: ' + e.message);
} finally {
    // runs no matter what — cleanup code goes here
}

// When to use try/catch:
// - Parsing JSON from external systems (malformed data)
// - REST API calls (network failures)
// - Any operation where bad data could crash your Business Rule

Scope — the #1 confusion point

// Variables declared with var inside a function are LOCAL to that function
function myFunction() {
    var localVar = 'only exists here';
    gs.info(localVar); // works
}
// gs.info(localVar); // ReferenceError — does not exist outside

// Variables declared outside any function are GLOBAL to the script
var globalVar = 'visible everywhere in this script';
function test() {
    gs.info(globalVar); // works — can see the outer variable
}

// In Business Rules, 'current' and 'previous' are provided by the platform.
// You do not declare them. They are injected into the script context:
(function executeRule(current, previous) {
    // current = the record being modified
    // previous = the record BEFORE your changes (null on insert)
    // Both are GlideRecord objects pointing to the current row
})(current, previous);

What does NOT work on the server

// These are browser/Node.js features. They do not exist on the ServiceNow server.

// setTimeout / setInterval — no timers on server
// setTimeout(function() { }, 1000); // does not exist

// console.log — use gs.info instead
// console.log('test'); // does not exist

// document / window / DOM — there is no browser on the server
// document.getElementById('test'); // does not exist

// fetch / XMLHttpRequest — use RESTMessageV2 instead
// fetch('https://api.example.com'); // does not exist

// require / import — use gs.include for Script Includes
// var lib = require('mylib'); // does not exist

// Promise / async / await — not available in global scope server scripts
// Use GlideHTTPRequest or synchronous REST calls

Quick reference: where to write each script type

I want to...Write a...Navigate to
Validate data before saveBefore Business RuleSystem Definition > Business Rules
Create related records after saveAfter Business RuleSystem Definition > Business Rules
Show/hide fields on a formClient Script (onLoad/onChange) or UI PolicySystem Definition > Client Scripts
Validate before form submitClient Script (onSubmit)System Definition > Client Scripts
Reusable server functionScript IncludeSystem Definition > Script Includes
Call server from clientGlideAjax + Script Include (extends AbstractAjaxProcessor)Both
Run something on a scheduleScheduled JobSystem Definition > Scheduled Jobs
One-time data cleanupFix Script or Background ScriptSystem Definition > Fix Scripts, or Scripts - Background
Custom button on a formUI ActionSystem Definition > UI Actions

title: Debugging ServiceNow: Session Debug, Slow Queries, Transaction Logs, and Script Tracing
excerpt: When something breaks in production and you have 10 minutes to find it. System diagnostics, session debug modules, transaction logs, and the logs that actually tell you what happened.
content:
Where to look first

When something is broken — a Business Rule is not firing, a form is slow, a notification is not sending — there are specific logs and tools for each problem. Do not guess. Go to the data.

ProblemWhere to lookNavigation path
Script errorsSystem Logs > Allsyslog_list.do
Slow forms/transactionsTransaction Logsyslog_transaction_list.do
Slow database queriesSlow Queriessys_slow_query_list.do
Email not sendingEmail Logsys_email_list.do
Business Rule not firingSession Debug > Business RuleSee below
ACL blocking accessSession Debug > SecuritySee below
Flow Designer errorsFlow Execution DetailsFlow Designer > Executions
Integration failuresOutbound HTTP logssys_outbound_http_log_list.do

Session Debug

Session Debug turns on detailed tracing for your current session. It does not affect other users. Enable it, reproduce the issue, then check the output in System Logs.

Enable via the System Diagnostics menu

// Navigate to: System Diagnostics > Session Debug > Enable All
// Or enable specific modules:
//   Debug Business Rule — shows which BRs fire, in what order, execution time
//   Debug Security Rules — shows ACL evaluation for every field/table access
//   Debug SQL — shows the raw SQL generated by GlideRecord queries
//   Debug Log — shows all gs.log/info/warn/error output

// After enabling, perform the action you want to debug (e.g., save an incident)
// Then check: System Logs > All (filter by your session)

What Debug Business Rule shows you

// Example output in System Logs after saving an incident:
// 
// === Business Rule: Set Priority (BEFORE, order 100) ===
// Table: incident
// Condition: priority changes
// Result: EXECUTED (4.2ms)
//
// === Business Rule: Auto-Assign (AFTER, order 200) ===
// Table: incident
// Condition: assignment_group is empty
// Result: SKIPPED (condition false)
//
// This tells you exactly which rules ran, which were skipped, and why.

What Debug Security shows you

// Example output when a user can't see a field:
//
// ACL: incident.caller_id (read)
// Role required: itil — PASS
// Condition: active=true — PASS
// Script: answer = ... — FAIL
// Result: DENIED
//
// Now you know exactly which ACL is blocking and which check failed.

System Logs

// Everything you write with gs.info, gs.warn, gs.error shows up here
// Filter by source to find your script's output:
gs.info('My debug output', 'MyScriptInclude');

// In the syslog table, filter:
//   Source = MyScriptInclude
//   Level = Info/Warning/Error
//   Created > last 10 minutes

Transaction Log

Every HTTP request to the instance is logged with timing data. When a form is slow, find the transaction here.

// Navigate to: syslog_transaction_list.do
// Key fields:
//   URL — which page/form/API was requested
//   Response time — total milliseconds
//   SQL count — number of database queries
//   Business Rule time — time spent in BRs
//
// Red flags:
//   Response time > 5000ms — slow transaction
//   SQL count > 100 — too many queries (N+1 problem likely)
//   Business Rule time > 2000ms — heavy BR logic

Slow Query Log

Queries that take longer than the threshold (default 500ms) are automatically logged here.

// Navigate to: sys_slow_query_list.do
// Key fields:
//   Table — which table was queried
//   Execution time — how long the query took
//   Source — which script/BR triggered it
//   Query — the encoded query string
//
// Common causes:
//   Missing index on a filtered field
//   No setLimit() on a large table query
//   Dot-walking through multiple reference fields
//   GlideRecord loop inside another GlideRecord loop (N+1)

Email debugging

// When a notification does not send, check these in order:
// 1. sys_email_list.do — is the email record created? What is its state?
//    States: ready, sent, send-failed, skipped
//
// 2. If state = skipped:
//    Check the notification's conditions and "Who will receive" config
//    Check if the user unsubscribed (notification_preference table)
//
// 3. If state = send-failed:
//    Check syslog for SMTP errors
//
// 4. In sub-production instances:
//    Check glide.email.test.user property — it redirects ALL email
//    to a single address. This is by design to prevent test emails
//    going to real users.

Script debugging without session debug

// Quick debugging pattern for Business Rules:
(function executeRule(current, previous) {
    // Temporarily add targeted logging
    gs.info('[BR:SetPriority] Fired on ' + current.number +
            ' | impact=' + current.getValue('impact') +
            ' | urgency=' + current.getValue('urgency') +
            ' | old_priority=' + (previous ? previous.getValue('priority') : 'N/A'));

    // Your logic here...

    gs.info('[BR:SetPriority] Result: priority set to ' + current.getValue('priority'));
})(current, previous);

// Find your logs: System Logs > All, filter Source CONTAINS SetPriority

Stats.do — Quick instance diagnostics

Navigate to your-instance.service-now.com/stats.do for a quick overview of instance health: memory usage, active transactions, semaphore counts, node status, and session counts. Useful during performance incidents when you need a fast read on whether the instance itself is under stress.

Common traps

  • Session debug left on: Debug sessions generate large amounts of log data. Always disable after you are done. Leaving it on in production degrades performance.
  • Logging sensitive data: gs.info writes to syslog which is visible to admins. Never log passwords, PII, or API keys.
  • Debug output not showing: If you enabled debug but see nothing, check that you are looking at the correct time window and that your script actually executed. Also verify you are on the correct node in a multi-node instance.
  • Transaction log vs slow query: A slow transaction does not always mean a slow query. The time could be in Business Rule execution, external REST calls, or Flow Designer actions. Check the breakdown columns.

title: Service Catalog Scripting: Record Producers, Variables, Catalog Client Scripts, and Order Guides
excerpt: Everything that happens between a user clicking 'Order Now' and the fulfillment task landing on someone's queue. Tables, variable types, catalog-specific scripts, and the gotchas that bite in production.
content:
How the catalog works internally

When a user submits a catalog item, ServiceNow creates three types of records:

TableRecord TypeWhat it represents
sc_requestRequestThe overall order (REQ0010001). One per submission.
sc_req_itemRequested Item (RITM)One per catalog item ordered (RITM0010001). Contains variable values.
sc_taskCatalog TaskFulfillment work assigned to teams (SCTASK0010001).

Variable values are stored in sc_item_option and linked to the RITM via sc_item_option_mtom.

Reading variable values in scripts

// In a Catalog Item workflow or Business Rule on sc_req_item:
var ritmGr = new GlideRecord('sc_req_item');
ritmGr.get('number', 'RITM0010001');

// Access variables through the variables object
var laptopModel = ritmGr.variables.laptop_model.getDisplayValue();
var justification = ritmGr.variables.justification.toString();

// In a Catalog Item script (server-side):
// 'current' is the RITM record
var model = current.variables.laptop_model;

Record Producers

A Record Producer creates a record on a target table (like incident) through the Service Catalog UI. The user fills out catalog-style variables, and the Record Producer maps them to fields on the target table.

// Record Producer script (runs on submit, server-side)
// 'current' is the target table record (e.g., incident)
// 'producer' has the variable values

current.short_description = producer.description;
current.category = producer.category;
current.priority = producer.urgency_level;

// Set caller to the person who submitted
current.caller_id = gs.getUserID();

When to use Record Producer vs Catalog Item:

  • Record Producer: When the goal is to create a record on an existing table (incident, change_request, etc.) from the catalog. The user sees a catalog form, but the output is a standard record, not a RITM.
  • Catalog Item: When you need the full request lifecycle (Request → RITM → Tasks) with approvals, fulfillment workflows, and catalog-specific tracking.

Variable Sets

A Variable Set is a reusable group of variables shared across multiple catalog items. Instead of creating the same "Delivery Address" fields on 15 different items, create one Variable Set and attach it to all of them.

// Variable sets are just containers — access their variables
// the same way via current.variables.variable_name

Catalog Client Scripts

These are Client Scripts that run specifically on catalog item forms. They have the same event types (onLoad, onChange, onSubmit) but operate on catalog variables instead of table fields.

// Catalog Client Script — onChange
// Variable: 'laptop_model'
function onChange(control, oldValue, newValue, isLoading) {
    if (isLoading) return;

    // Show/hide the 'special_requirements' variable based on model
    if (newValue === 'MacBook Pro 16') {
        g_form.setVisible('special_requirements', true);
        g_form.setMandatory('special_requirements', true);
    } else {
        g_form.setVisible('special_requirements', false);
        g_form.setMandatory('special_requirements', false);
    }
}

// Catalog Client Script — onSubmit
function onSubmit() {
    var model = g_form.getValue('laptop_model');
    var justification = g_form.getValue('justification');

    if (model === 'MacBook Pro 16' && !justification) {
        g_form.addErrorMessage('Justification required for MacBook Pro 16.');
        return false;  // prevent submission
    }
    return true;
}

Catalog UI Policy

Same concept as a regular UI Policy but scoped to catalog variables. Controls visibility, mandatory state, and read-only state of catalog variables without code.

When Laptop Model = "MacBook Pro 16" → make Special Requirements mandatory. Configured entirely through the UI, no JavaScript needed.

Order Guides

An Order Guide bundles multiple catalog items into a single guided ordering experience. The user walks through steps, and at the end, multiple RITMs are created.

Order Guide scripts can pre-populate variables on child items based on selections in earlier steps:

// Order Guide Rule script — maps a variable from the guide to child items
// 'guide_variables' holds the Order Guide level variables
// 'item_variables' holds the current item's variables

item_variables.delivery_location = guide_variables.office_location;
item_variables.cost_center = guide_variables.department_cost_center;

Common traps

  • Catalog Client Scripts vs regular Client Scripts: Catalog Client Scripts only run on catalog forms. Regular Client Scripts on sc_req_item run on the RITM form, not the catalog order form. These are different contexts.
  • Variable names vs labels: In scripts, use the variable name (e.g., laptop_model), not the label ("Laptop Model"). The name is set when you create the variable and cannot contain spaces.
  • Two-step variable access: current.variables.var_name in server-side scripts, g_form.getValue('var_name') in client-side scripts. They look different but access the same data.
  • Multi-row variable sets (MRVS): These store tabular data and are accessed differently — current.variables.mvrs_name.getRowCount() and iterating rows. They do not work like regular variables.

title: Server-Side Utility APIs You Use Every Day: GlideDateTime, GlideElement, gs Methods
excerpt: The utility APIs that show up in every Business Rule and Script Include but nobody explains in one place. Date math, field inspection, system properties, and logging.
content:
GlideDateTime — Date and time operations

ServiceNow stores dates in UTC internally. GlideDateTime handles timezone conversion, date math, and formatting.

// Current date/time
var now = new GlideDateTime();
gs.info(now.getValue());        // '2026-04-07 14:30:00' (UTC, internal)
gs.info(now.getDisplayValue()); // '2026-04-07 09:30:00' (user's timezone)

// Create from string
var dt = new GlideDateTime('2026-01-15 08:00:00');

// Date math — add/subtract
var dt = new GlideDateTime();
dt.addDaysUTC(7);               // add 7 days
dt.addSeconds(3600);             // add 1 hour
dt.addYearsUTC(1);               // add 1 year

// Compare dates
var dt1 = new GlideDateTime('2026-01-01 00:00:00');
var dt2 = new GlideDateTime('2026-06-01 00:00:00');
gs.info(dt1.before(dt2));       // true
gs.info(dt1.after(dt2));        // false

// Difference between dates
var diff = GlideDateTime.subtract(dt1, dt2);  // returns GlideDuration
gs.info(diff.getDayPart());     // number of days between

// Get parts
gs.info(now.getYearUTC());      // 2026
gs.info(now.getMonthUTC());     // 4
gs.info(now.getDayOfMonthUTC()); // 7

// gs date helpers — quick shortcuts
gs.info(gs.now());              // current date/time in user's format
gs.info(gs.nowDateTime());      // current date/time in system format
gs.info(gs.daysAgo(7));         // date/time 7 days ago
gs.info(gs.beginningOfLastMonth()); // first day of previous month

GlideElement — Field-level operations

When you access gr.field_name on a GlideRecord, you get a GlideElement object, not a raw value. These methods let you inspect and manipulate individual fields.

var gr = new GlideRecord('incident');
gr.get('number', 'INC0010001');

// Check if a field changed (only works in Business Rules with 'previous')
if (gr.priority.changes()) {
    gs.info('Priority changed');
}

// Check if field changed TO a specific value
if (gr.state.changesTo(6)) {
    gs.info('State changed to Resolved');
}

// Check if field changed FROM a specific value
if (gr.state.changesFrom(1)) {
    gs.info('State was previously New');
}

// Check if a field is empty
if (gr.assigned_to.nil()) {
    gs.info('No one assigned');
}
// gs.nil() works the same way
if (gs.nil(gr.getValue('assigned_to'))) {
    gs.info('Also no one assigned');
}

// Get the field's label (not the column name)
gs.info(gr.priority.getLabel());  // 'Priority'

// Get choice list display value
gs.info(gr.priority.getDisplayValue());  // '1 - Critical'

// Reference field helpers
gs.info(gr.caller_id.getRefRecord().getValue('email'));  // get the referenced record

gs (GlideSystem) — System utilities

Logging

gs.info('Informational message');           // System Logs > All
gs.warn('Warning message');                  // shows as warning level
gs.error('Error message');                   // shows as error level
gs.debug('Debug message');                   // only shows when debug enabled

// Log with source context (appears in Source column)
gs.log('message', 'MyScriptInclude');        // legacy, use gs.info instead

User context

gs.info(gs.getUserID());          // sys_id of current user
gs.info(gs.getUserName());        // 'john.smith'
gs.info(gs.getUserDisplayName()); // 'John Smith'
gs.info(gs.getUser().getEmail()); // 'john@example.com'

// Check roles (server-side)
if (gs.hasRole('admin')) { }
if (gs.hasRole('itil')) { }

System properties

// Read a system property
var val = gs.getProperty('glide.servlet.uri');  // instance URL
var custom = gs.getProperty('x_myapp.feature_flag', 'default_value');

// Set a system property (use carefully)
gs.setProperty('x_myapp.last_sync', gs.nowDateTime());

Messages and events

// Show messages to the user (in Business Rules)
gs.addInfoMessage('Record saved successfully.');
gs.addErrorMessage('Cannot close without resolution notes.');

// Queue an event (for notifications, flows, or custom processing)
gs.eventQueue('incident.escalated', current, gs.getUserID(), current.getValue('assignment_group'));

// Prefer instantiating the Script Include (Class.create pattern).
// gs.include('MyUtilityLibrary') still exists for older includes, but
// new MyUtilityLibrary() is the usual modern call site.
var utils = new MyUtilityLibrary();

Data Policy vs UI Policy

Both control field mandatory/read-only behavior, but at different layers:

FeatureUI PolicyData Policy
Runs onClient (browser) onlyServer + Client
Enforced via APINo — only on the formYes — REST, import, scripts all respect it
ConfigurationUI-only, no codeUI-only, no code
Use whenForm-only field behaviorData integrity regardless of entry point

If a field must always be mandatory — even for records created via API or Import Set — use a Data Policy. If it only matters when a user is filling out a form, UI Policy is sufficient.

Common traps

  • GlideDateTime timezone confusion: getValue() returns UTC, getDisplayValue() returns the user's timezone. When comparing dates in scripts, always use getValue() or UTC methods.
  • gr.field.nil() vs gs.nil(): Both work, but gs.nil() also handles null, undefined, and empty strings. Prefer gs.nil(gr.getValue('field')) for defensive coding.
  • gs.getProperty() performance: System properties are cached, so repeated calls are fast. But do not call gs.getProperty() inside a tight loop on a high-volume table — read it once and store it in a variable.
  • gs.addInfoMessage in async Business Rules: Will not display. The user's transaction is already complete. Only works in before/after BRs where the form is still in context.

title: ServiceNow Client-Side APIs: g_form, g_user, g_list — The Methods That Control the Form
excerpt: Complete reference for the three client-side objects you use in every Client Script and UI Action. Every method, what it returns, and when it breaks.
content:
Where these run

Client-side scripts run in the user's browser, not on the server. You cannot use GlideRecord here. The three objects available to you are:

  • g_form — manipulates the current form (fields, labels, messages)
  • g_user — information about the logged-in user
  • g_list — manipulates list views (less common)

g_form — Form manipulation

Get and set field values

// Get the raw value (sys_id for reference fields, number for choice fields)
var callerId = g_form.getValue('caller_id');       // sys_id string
var priority = g_form.getValue('priority');         // '1'

// Get the display value (the text the user sees)
var callerName = g_form.getDisplayValue('caller_id'); // 'John Smith'

// Set a field value
g_form.setValue('priority', '2');
g_form.setValue('assignment_group', 'a1b2c3d4...');  // must be sys_id for reference fields

// Clear a field
g_form.clearValue('assigned_to');

Control field visibility and behavior

// Hide/show a field
g_form.setVisible('u_internal_notes', false);  // hide
g_form.setVisible('u_internal_notes', true);   // show

// Make a field mandatory
g_form.setMandatory('assignment_group', true);

// Make a field read-only
g_form.setReadOnly('short_description', true);

// Set a field label (useful for dynamic labels)
g_form.setLabelOf('u_custom_field', 'New Label Text');

Messages on the form

// Info message (blue banner at top)
g_form.addInfoMessage('This incident has been escalated.');

// Error message (red banner at top)
g_form.addErrorMessage('Missing required data.');

// Field-level message (appears under a specific field)
g_form.showFieldMsg('short_description', 'Must be at least 10 characters', 'error');
g_form.hideFieldMsg('short_description');

// Clear all messages
g_form.clearMessages();

Form state

// Check if the form is for a new record
if (g_form.isNewRecord()) {
    // This is an insert, not an update
}

// Get the table name
var table = g_form.getTableName();  // 'incident'

// Get the sys_id of the current record
var sysId = g_form.getUniqueValue();

// Check if a field value has changed (useful in onChange)
var changed = g_form.isFieldChanged('priority');  // only works in onChange context

// Submit the form programmatically
g_form.submit();

Reference field lookups (getReference)

// getReference is asynchronous — always use the callback form
g_form.getReference('caller_id', function(callerRecord) {
    // callerRecord is a GlideRecord-like object
    var dept = callerRecord.department.getDisplayValue();
    g_form.addInfoMessage('Caller department: ' + dept);
});

// NEVER use the synchronous form — it freezes the browser
// var ref = g_form.getReference('caller_id'); // BAD — blocks UI

g_user — Current user information

// Basic user info
var userName = g_user.userName;      // 'john.smith'
var fullName = g_user.getFullName(); // 'John Smith'
var userId   = g_user.userID;        // sys_id of the logged-in user

// Role checks
if (g_user.hasRole('admin')) {
    // user has admin role
}
if (g_user.hasRole('itil')) {
    // user has ITIL role
}
// hasRoleExactly checks the specific role, not inherited roles
if (g_user.hasRoleExactly('incident_manager')) {
    // user has incident_manager specifically, not just admin
}

// Client-side data from g_user.getClientData (set in Display Business Rule)
// In Display BR:  g_scratchpad.isVIP = true;
// In Client Script: var isVIP = g_scratchpad.isVIP;

g_scratchpad — Pass server data to client

g_scratchpad is an object populated by Display Business Rules on the server side, then available in Client Scripts. This is the correct way to pass server data to the client without making GlideAjax calls.

// === Display Business Rule (server-side, runs when form loads) ===
(function executeRule(current, previous) {
    g_scratchpad.callerIsVIP = current.caller_id.vip.toString();
    g_scratchpad.openP1Count = new GlideAggregate('incident');
    // ... calculate value ...
    g_scratchpad.openP1Count = '5';
})(current, previous);

// === Client Script (onLoad, runs in browser) ===
function onLoad() {
    if (g_scratchpad.callerIsVIP === 'true') {
        g_form.addInfoMessage('VIP caller — handle with priority.');
    }
}

g_list — List view manipulation

Available only in list context (not forms). Less commonly used but important for UI Actions on lists.

// Get selected sys_ids from a list (checkboxes)
var selectedIds = g_list.getChecked();  // comma-separated sys_ids

// Refresh the current list
g_list.refresh();

// Get the list's table name
var table = g_list.getTableName();

// Get the current list filter (encoded query)
var filter = g_list.getQuery();

Common traps

  • Using GlideRecord in a Client Script: It does not exist on the client side. Use GlideAjax to call a Script Include on the server if you need database access.
  • Synchronous getReference: The no-callback version of g_form.getReference() blocks the browser's main thread. Always pass a callback function.
  • g_user.hasRole('admin') returns true for admins on everything: Admin role bypasses all role checks. If you want to check a specific role without admin bypass, use g_user.hasRoleExactly().
  • setValue on reference fields: You must pass a sys_id, not a display name. To set by display name, use g_form.getReference() first or pass both: there is no two-arg version for setValue reference, so you need the sys_id.
  • UI Policies override Client Scripts: If both control the same field, the UI Policy runs after the Client Script and wins. Do not use both on the same field unless you understand the execution order.

title: GlideRecord Complete Reference: Every Method You Actually Use in Production
excerpt: The one GlideRecord page you bookmark. Query, insert, update, delete patterns with real output, performance traps, and the methods nobody explains properly.
content:
What GlideRecord is

GlideRecord is the server-side JavaScript API for reading and writing database records in ServiceNow. Every Business Rule, Script Include, Scheduled Job, and Fix Script you write will use it. Think of it as a cursor-based query builder — you build a query, execute it, then iterate row by row.

Query (SELECT)

var gr = new GlideRecord('incident');
gr.addQuery('priority', 1);
gr.addQuery('state', '!=', 6);            // 6 = Resolved
gr.addQuery('assignment_group.name', 'Network Ops');  // dot-walk through reference
gr.orderByDesc('sys_created_on');
gr.setLimit(20);
gr.query();

while (gr.next()) {
    gs.info(gr.getValue('number'));           // INC0010045
    gs.info(gr.getDisplayValue('caller_id')); // John Smith
    gs.info(gr.getValue('caller_id'));        // 6816f79cc0a8016401... (sys_id)
}

What actually happens: query() sends SQL to the database. next() moves the cursor to the next row. When there are no more rows, next() returns false and the loop ends.

addQuery operators

OperatorExampleWhat it does
=addQuery('priority', 1)Exact match (default)
!=addQuery('state', '!=', 6)Not equal
>addQuery('sys_created_on', '>', '2026-01-01')Greater than
<addQuery('priority', '<', 3)Less than
INaddQuery('state', 'IN', '1,2,3')Value in comma-separated list
NOT INaddQuery('state', 'NOT IN', '6,7')Value not in list
STARTSWITHaddQuery('number', 'STARTSWITH', 'INC')String starts with
CONTAINSaddQuery('short_description', 'CONTAINS', 'VPN')String contains
ISEMPTY / nulladdNullQuery('assigned_to')Field is null/empty (prefer addNullQuery in script)
ISNOTEMPTYaddNotNullQuery('assigned_to')Field has a value

OR queries

var gr = new GlideRecord('incident');
var q1 = gr.addQuery('priority', 1);
q1.addOrCondition('priority', 2);   // priority = 1 OR priority = 2
gr.query();

Encoded queries

Instead of chaining addQuery calls, paste the encoded query string directly. Copy it from any list filter in the UI — click the filter icon, set your conditions, right-click the breadcrumb, and select "Copy query."

var gr = new GlideRecord('incident');
gr.addEncodedQuery('priority=1^stateNOT IN6,7^assignment_group.name=Network Ops');
gr.query();

// This does the same thing as the three addQuery calls above.
// Encoded queries are faster to write and easier to paste from the UI.

Get a single record

// By sys_id
var gr = new GlideRecord('incident');
gr.get('a1b2c3d4e5f6a7b8c9d0e1f2a3b4c5d6');

// By field value
var gr = new GlideRecord('incident');
gr.get('number', 'INC0010001');

// gr.get() returns true/false. No need to call query() or next().

Insert

var gr = new GlideRecord('incident');
gr.initialize();
gr.short_description = 'Printer offline on floor 3';
gr.priority = 3;
gr.assignment_group.setDisplayValue('Service Desk');  // look up by name
var newSysId = gr.insert();  // returns the sys_id of the new record
gs.info('Created: ' + newSysId);

Update

var gr = new GlideRecord('incident');
gr.get('number', 'INC0010001');
gr.state = 6;  // Resolved
gr.close_notes = 'Restarted the print spooler service.';
gr.update();

Bulk update

// Close all resolved incidents older than 7 days
var gr = new GlideRecord('incident');
gr.addQuery('state', 6);
gr.addQuery('resolved_at', '<', gs.daysAgo(7));
gr.query();
while (gr.next()) {
    gr.state = 7;  // Closed
    gr.update();
}
// For large volumes, use gr.setWorkflow(false) to skip Business Rules
// and gr.autoSysFields(false) to skip sys_updated_on/by changes.

Delete

var gr = new GlideRecord('incident');
gr.get('number', 'INC9999999');
gr.deleteRecord();

// Bulk delete — be very careful
var gr = new GlideRecord('u_temp_import');
gr.addQuery('sys_created_on', '<', gs.daysAgo(30));
gr.deleteMultiple();  // Deletes all matching records without loading them

getValue vs getDisplayValue vs dot notation

MethodReturnsUse when
gr.getValue('caller_id')sys_id stringComparisons, integrations, storing references
gr.getDisplayValue('caller_id')Display nameMessages, emails, UI display
gr.caller_idGlideElement objectAvoid — behaves unpredictably in comparisons
gr.getValue('state')'1' (internal number)Logic, conditions
gr.getDisplayValue('state')'New' (label)Display only — labels change with language

GlideAggregate

When you need COUNT, SUM, MIN, MAX, or AVG — do not loop through GlideRecord and count manually.

// Count open P1 incidents
var ga = new GlideAggregate('incident');
ga.addQuery('priority', 1);
ga.addQuery('active', true);
ga.addAggregate('COUNT');
ga.query();
if (ga.next()) {
    gs.info('Open P1 count: ' + ga.getAggregate('COUNT'));
}

// Count per assignment group
var ga = new GlideAggregate('incident');
ga.addQuery('active', true);
ga.addAggregate('COUNT');
ga.groupBy('assignment_group');
ga.query();
while (ga.next()) {
    gs.info(ga.getDisplayValue('assignment_group') + ': ' + ga.getAggregate('COUNT'));
}

Common traps

  • Querying the task table: new GlideRecord('task') returns incidents + changes + problems + catalog tasks + everything else that extends task. Always query the specific child table unless you genuinely want all task types.
  • getRowCount(): Runs a full COUNT(*) against the database. On tables with millions of rows, this is expensive. Use GlideAggregate instead.
  • Dot-walking in loops: gr.caller_id.department.name fires a separate query per iteration. For bulk operations, query the related table separately and build a lookup map.
  • Missing setLimit(): Without a limit, your query can return hundreds of thousands of rows. Always set a limit unless you specifically need all records.
  • gr.field = value vs gr.setValue('field', value): Both work for most fields, but setValue is safer for reference fields and journal fields. Use setValue in script includes; direct assignment in business rules is fine.

title: ServiceNow AI Buzzwords Explained (Easy): AI Agents, Agentic AI, AI Control Tower, RaptorDB, and More
excerpt: A beginner-friendly enterprise guide to 15 major ServiceNow AI terms with practical examples and when each term matters.
content:
Why This Guide Exists

ServiceNow's AI conversations are full of fast-moving terms that change with every release. Marketing materials use "agentic AI," "AI Control Tower," and "Workflow Data Fabric" without explaining what they actually mean for someone configuring the platform.

This guide translates every major ServiceNow AI buzzword from marketing language to practical understanding. For each term, you get: what it is in plain English, what it actually does in the platform, and when you would use it.

The Complete Buzzword Map

BuzzwordPlain English MeaningWhat It Does in ServiceNowWhen You Care About It
Now AssistAI assistant embedded in ServiceNow workflowsSummarizes tickets, drafts responses, generates code, recommends solutions — all inside the platform UIImmediately — this is the most visible AI feature for users and agents
AI AgentsAI workers that can execute multi-step tasks autonomouslyCan handle end-to-end request fulfillment: read a ticket, check policies, take action, update the record, notify the userAfter Now Assist is stable — AI Agents are the next evolution for automating routine tasks
Agentic AIAI that plans and takes actions (not just answers questions)The underlying paradigm for AI Agents — AI that reasons about what steps to take, executes them, and handles errorsArchitecture discussions — this is the "why" behind AI Agents
AI Agent StudioBuilder tool for creating and configuring AI AgentsVisual interface where you define what an AI Agent can do, which tools it can use, and what guardrails applyWhen you are ready to build custom AI Agents beyond the out-of-box ones
AI Agent FabricOrchestration layer for multiple AI agents working togetherCoordinates when a Security agent, IT agent, and HR agent need to collaborate on a cross-domain issueAdvanced deployments with multiple specialized agents
AI Control TowerGovernance dashboard for all AI activityShows which AI models are in use, what decisions they are making, compliance status, risk scores, and usage analyticsCompliance and governance teams — required for regulated industries
Now LLMServiceNow's own Large Language ModelThe AI model that powers Now Assist skills. Hosted on ServiceNow infrastructure so your data does not leave the platform boundary.Security and architecture discussions — "where does the AI processing happen?"
Workflow Data FabricUnified data access layer across all ServiceNow dataLets AI access data from ITSM, HRSD, CSM, CMDB, and custom apps through one interface — no separate queries per moduleWhen AI needs cross-domain context (e.g., "this P1 incident affects a VIP employee who also has an open HR case")
Knowledge GraphRelationship-aware knowledge structureConnects services, CIs, KB articles, incidents, owners, and teams into a web of relationships — AI uses this to find relevant context that simple keyword search would missNow Assist quality improvements — a Knowledge Graph gives AI richer context for better answers
RaptorDBHigh-performance database engine for ServiceNowA new database layer that dramatically speeds up reporting, analytics, and large-scale queries. Not an AI feature itself, but enables AI features to process data faster.Performance — if your instance is slow with large datasets, RaptorDB is the infrastructure upgrade
Predictive IntelligenceML models that predict outcomes from historical patternsAuto-categorize incidents, predict assignment groups, identify similar incidents, forecast resolution times — all based on patterns in your historical dataBefore or alongside Now Assist — Predictive Intelligence uses traditional ML, not generative AI
Virtual AgentConversational chatbot for self-serviceUsers chat with a bot in the portal or messaging apps (Teams, Slack). The bot understands intent, asks clarifying questions, and either resolves the issue or creates a ticket with pre-filled data.Self-service strategy — Virtual Agent is the front door for employee requests
Document IntelligenceAI-powered document processing (OCR + ML)Extracts structured data from scanned documents, PDFs, and images — ID cards, invoices, contracts — and populates ServiceNow fields automaticallyHR onboarding, procurement, and any workflow that involves processing paper or PDF documents
Zero-Copy Data AccessAccess external data without importing itQuery data lakes, data warehouses, or external databases from inside ServiceNow workflows — without copying the data into ServiceNow tablesIntegration architecture — when you need external data for AI context but cannot replicate it
Autonomous WorkflowA workflow that runs end-to-end without human interventionCombines AI Agents + Flow Designer + Predictive Intelligence to handle routine requests (password resets, software access) completely automaticallyThe end goal of AI automation — start with Now Assist, evolve to AI Agents, target autonomous resolution for routine tasks
Governed AIAI that operates under policy, audit, and risk controlsEvery AI action is logged, auditable, and subject to organizational policies. AI Control Tower provides the governance layer.Compliance, risk management, and any regulated industry deployment
Skill KitToolkit for building custom Now Assist skillsWhen the out-of-box skills do not cover your use case, the Skill Kit lets you build custom AI skills — define your own prompts, connect your own data sources, and deploy them in the Now Assist panelWhen you need AI capabilities beyond what comes out of the box (e.g., summarize a custom table, generate a specialized report)
Generative AI ControllerPolicy engine for controlling GenAI behaviorDefines rules for what generative AI can and cannot do: allowed topics, blocked content, PII handling, response length limits. Centralized policy management for all GenAI features.Security and governance setup — configure before enabling Now Assist at scale

How These Terms Fit Together

These are not isolated features — they form layers of an AI stack:

┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  EXPERIENCE LAYER (what users see)                    │
│  Now Assist · Virtual Agent · AI Search               │
├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  AGENT LAYER (autonomous work)                        │
│  AI Agents · AI Agent Studio · AI Agent Fabric        │
├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  INTELLIGENCE LAYER (AI models and reasoning)         │
│  Now LLM · Predictive Intelligence · Document Intel   │
│  Knowledge Graph · Skill Kit                          │
├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  DATA LAYER (context for AI decisions)                │
│  Workflow Data Fabric · CMDB · Knowledge Base         │
│  Zero-Copy Data Access · RaptorDB                     │
├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  GOVERNANCE LAYER (controls and compliance)           │
│  AI Control Tower · Generative AI Controller          │
│  Governed AI · Audit Trails                           │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Read it bottom to top: Governance sets the rules. Data provides the context. Intelligence runs the models. Agents take autonomous action. Experience is what the end user sees.

Practical Interpretation — What Each Term Means for Your Role

If You Are a System Administrator

Your primary concerns: Now Assist (enable and configure skills), Virtual Agent (manage topics and conversations), Predictive Intelligence (configure ML models for categorization and assignment), Now Assist Admin Console (your daily hub for AI management).

If You Are a Developer

Your primary concerns: Skill Kit (build custom Now Assist skills), AI Agent Studio (create AI Agents), Now Assist for Creator (use AI to generate code and flows), Flow Designer integration with AI actions.

If You Are an Architect

Your primary concerns: Workflow Data Fabric (data strategy for AI), AI Agent Fabric (multi-agent orchestration), Knowledge Graph (data model for AI context), RaptorDB (performance), Zero-Copy Data Access (integration architecture).

If You Are in Leadership / Governance

Your primary concerns: AI Control Tower (visibility and compliance), Governed AI (policy enforcement), Generative AI Controller (guardrails), Autonomous Workflow (ROI and automation targets).

The Implementation Sequence That Works

Do not try to adopt everything at once. Here is the proven order:

  1. Clean your data foundation — CMDB, KB articles, categorization, work note quality
  2. Enable Predictive Intelligence — auto-categorize, auto-assign. This uses traditional ML and gives quick wins.
  3. Deploy Virtual Agent — self-service chatbot for common requests (password reset, VPN help, software access)
  4. Enable Now Assist skills — start with summarization and resolution notes for agents
  5. Build custom skills — use the Skill Kit for organization-specific AI capabilities
  6. Deploy AI Agents — autonomous task execution for routine, well-defined workflows
  7. Activate AI Control Tower — governance and monitoring for the entire AI stack
  8. Expand with Knowledge Graph and Workflow Data Fabric — richer context for better AI decisions

title: What is ServiceNow Now Assist? A Beginner Guide with Real Enterprise Examples
excerpt: Understand Now Assist in simple terms: where it helps, where it does not, and how enterprises measure real value.
content:
Now Assist in Plain English

If you have used ChatGPT, Copilot, or any AI assistant at home, you already understand the basic idea behind Now Assist. Now Assist is ServiceNow's built-in AI assistant that helps employees and support agents work faster by summarizing information, suggesting responses, generating content, and finding answers — all within the ServiceNow platform they already use every day.

The critical distinction: Now Assist is not a separate chatbot you deploy and maintain. It is embedded directly inside ServiceNow workflows — inside the incident form, the knowledge base, the service catalog, the HR case, the customer service interaction. When an agent opens a ticket, AI suggestions appear right there. When an employee searches the portal, AI-enhanced answers appear automatically. There is no separate tool to log into.

The Simplest Way to Think About It

Think of Now Assist as three AI assistants in one:

AssistantWho It HelpsWhat It DoesReal Example
Agent AssistSupport agents (IT, HR, Customer Service)Summarizes case history, suggests responses, drafts resolution notes, recommends similar past incidentsAn L1 agent opens a ticket with 47 comments spanning 3 weeks. Instead of reading everything, they click "Summarize" and get a 5-line summary of the issue, actions taken, and current status in 3 seconds.
Requester AssistEmployees / End usersHelps people find answers and submit better requests through the self-service portalAn employee types "my VPN is not connecting" in the portal. Instead of just showing search results, Now Assist generates a direct answer: "Try these 3 steps first..." with a link to the full KB article.
Creator AssistDevelopers and admins building on the platformGenerates code, flows, catalog items, and playbooks from natural language descriptionsA developer types "create a flow that sends a Slack notification when a P1 incident is created" and Now Assist generates the Flow Designer configuration.

Every Now Assist Skill — What It Actually Does

Now Assist is organized into skills — individual AI capabilities that can be turned on or off per module. Think of skills like apps on your phone: you enable the ones you need.

The skills fall into four families. ITSM skills help IT agents: incident, chat, and change summarization, resolution notes generation, KB article generation, and suggested chat replies. HRSD and CSM skills apply the same ideas to HR cases and customer cases, adding CSM-specific capabilities like email reply drafting and voice call summarization. Creator skills help builders: flow generation, code assist, and catalog item, playbook, app, and dashboard generation from natural language.

For the full skill-by-skill breakdown — what each skill does, where it appears in the UI, and how to configure it — see the companion post "Now Assist Skills Deep Dive: Every Skill, Every Module, and How to Set Them Up" on this blog.

How Now Assist Works Under the Hood

Understanding the architecture helps you troubleshoot when AI suggestions are poor and explain to stakeholders why certain things work or do not work.

The Flow of an AI Request

User clicks "Summarize" on an incident
        ↓
Now Assist reads the incident data:
  - Work notes, comments, activity log
  - Related records (tasks, CIs, changes)
  - Knowledge articles linked to the incident
        ↓
ServiceNow constructs a prompt:
  - System instructions + context data + user request
  - Guardrails applied (PII filtering, topic restrictions)
        ↓
Prompt sent to LLM (Large Language Model):
  - ServiceNow's own LLM infrastructure (Now LLM)
  - OR configured third-party model (Azure OpenAI)
        ↓
LLM generates response
        ↓
Response filtered through guardrails:
  - PII detection, harmful content check
  - Relevance verification
        ↓
Summary displayed to user in the Now Assist panel
  - User can accept, edit, or dismiss

Key Architecture Concepts

ConceptWhat It MeansWhy It Matters
Now LLMServiceNow's own large language model, hosted on ServiceNow infrastructureYour data stays within ServiceNow's boundary — no third-party data exposure. This matters for compliance-sensitive industries (healthcare, finance, government).
SkillsIndividual AI capabilities that can be enabled/disabled per moduleYou control exactly which AI features are active. Enable summarization for ITSM but not for HRSD if you want to phase the rollout.
GuardrailsRules that filter what goes into prompts and what comes out of responsesPrevents the AI from exposing PII (names, SSNs, emails) in generated text and blocks off-topic or harmful content.
Context GroundingThe AI response is grounded in actual ServiceNow data (incident notes, KB articles), not just general knowledgeReduces hallucination — the AI cites actual records instead of making things up. This is why clean data matters: garbage in = garbage out.
Now Assist Admin ConsoleThe centralized administration hub where you manage all AI settingsOne place to enable skills, review usage analytics, configure guardrails, and manage LLM connections.

Setting Up Now Assist — Step by Step

This is the practical setup path for a ServiceNow admin enabling Now Assist for the first time:

Step 1: Verify Your Instance Version

// Navigate to: your-instance.service-now.com/stats.do
// Check "Build name" on stats.do — Australia is the current family.
// Now Assist skills began shipping in earlier releases and expand each family
// (Skill Kit, AI Agents, AI Control Tower). Confirm which skills ship on your build
// via the release notes for that family.

Step 2: Open the Now Assist Admin Console

// Navigate to: All > Now Assist > Now Assist Admin
// This is the central hub for all AI configuration.
//
// What you will see:
// - Dashboard: usage metrics, active skills, model status
// - Skills: list of available skills by module (ITSM, HRSD, CSM, Creator)
// - Settings: plugin management, LLM configuration, data sharing controls
// - Analytics: how often skills are used, acceptance rates, feedback

Step 3: Install the Now Assist Applications

// Now Assist capabilities ship as applications, not classic plugins.
// Install the one for each workflow you own:
//   Now Assist for ITSM     → incident summary, resolution notes
//   Now Assist for HRSD     → HR case summary
//   Now Assist for CSM      → customer case summary, email reply
//   Now Assist for Creator  → code assist, flow generation
//
// Install and update them from the ServiceNow Store, or on the
// instance via System Applications > Application Manager.
// The Now Assist Admin console manages them once installed and licensed.

Step 4: Enable Your First Skills

// In the Now Assist Admin Console:
// 1. Go to the Skills section
// 2. Find "Incident Summarization" (a good first skill — low risk, high visibility)
// 3. Click to enable
// 4. Configure:
//    - Which roles can use it (e.g., itil, admin)
//    - Whether it auto-runs or requires user click
//    - Any additional guardrail settings
// 5. Save and test with a sample incident

Step 5: Test and Validate

// Open an incident with a substantial work note history
// Look for the Now Assist panel (usually right side of the form)
// Click "Summarize"
// Review the generated summary:
//   - Is it accurate?
//   - Does it capture the key points?
//   - Does it expose any sensitive data it shouldn't?
// If satisfied, expand to more users; if not, check data quality.

Where Teams Get Confused — Common Misconceptions

MisconceptionReality
"Now Assist will fix our broken processes"AI amplifies what you already have. If your incident categorization is a mess, AI suggestions will be a mess. Fix processes first, then add AI.
"We need to train the AI on our data"Now Assist uses pre-trained models plus your instance data as context. You do not train a custom model — you configure skills and ensure your data (KB articles, work notes) is clean and complete.
"Now Assist replaces L1 support agents"It augments them. Agents still review, approve, and edit AI-generated content. Now Assist handles the tedious parts (reading 50 comments, drafting notes) so agents can focus on judgment and empathy.
"AI suggestions are always accurate"They are usually helpful but not always correct. That is why every AI output has an accept/edit/dismiss option. Treat AI suggestions like a junior colleague's draft — review before using.
"We can enable everything at once"Phased rollout is critical. Start with 1-2 high-volume, low-risk skills (like incident summarization), measure results, then expand. Trying to enable all skills on day one overwhelms users and makes it impossible to measure impact.

The Data Quality Foundation

This is the single most important factor in Now Assist success. The AI generates responses based on what is in your ServiceNow data. If your data is poor, the AI output will be poor.

Data AreaWhat "Good" Looks LikeWhat "Bad" Looks LikeImpact on Now Assist
Work NotesDetailed, timestamped notes describing what was done and why at each stepEmpty or one-word notes like "done" or "fixed"Summarization is only as good as the notes. No notes = nothing to summarize.
Knowledge BaseWell-structured articles with clear steps, updated regularly, covering common issuesOutdated, incomplete, or nonexistent KB articlesKB Generation and Search Assist depend on existing knowledge quality. AI cannot create good articles from nothing.
CategorizationConsistent use of categories and subcategories with clear definitionsIncidents miscategorized or left as "Other/General"AI recommendations for routing and resolution depend on pattern matching against historical data. Bad categorization = bad patterns.
Resolution NotesClear description of what fixed the issue and what the root cause wasCopy-paste of the short description or "Resolved per user"Resolution Notes Generation learns from past closures. If past closures are garbage, generated notes will be too.

The #1 Rule of Now Assist

AI quality follows data quality. Before enabling Now Assist, audit your knowledge base, work note practices, and categorization standards. Spend 2 weeks cleaning data before spending 2 days enabling skills. The ROI difference is dramatic.

Measuring Success — What Leadership Cares About

MetricWhat It MeasuresHow to Track in ServiceNowTarget Benchmark
Average Handle Time (AHT)Time agents spend per ticketPerformance Analytics indicator on incident table15-30% reduction after Now Assist adoption
First Contact Resolution (FCR)Percentage of tickets resolved on first interactionReport: resolved_at within first assignment period5-10% improvement
Self-Service DeflectionTickets avoided because users found answers in portal/KBVirtual Agent + KB feedback analytics20-40% deflection rate for enabled categories
Agent SatisfactionHow agents feel about the AI toolsPost-shift surveys, feedback button on Now Assist panel70%+ positive feedback
AI Acceptance RateHow often agents accept AI suggestions vs. dismiss themNow Assist Admin Console analyticsAbove 60% suggests good quality; below 30% suggests data quality issues
Knowledge Article CoveragePercentage of common issues covered by KB articlesMap top 50 incident categories to existing KB articles80%+ coverage for top categories

Implementation Roadmap — Phased Approach

PhaseDurationWhat You DoSuccess Criteria
Phase 0: Foundation2-4 weeksAudit data quality. Clean KB articles. Standardize work note practices. Baseline current metrics (AHT, FCR, deflection).Top 20 incident categories have KB articles. Work note compliance above 80%.
Phase 1: Pilot4-6 weeksEnable 1-2 skills (start with Incident Summarization and Resolution Notes) for a pilot group of 10-20 agents.AI acceptance rate above 50%. Agents report time savings. No data quality issues flagged.
Phase 2: Expand6-8 weeksEnable for all ITSM agents. Add Chat Summarization and KB Generation. Start CSM or HRSD pilot if applicable.AHT reduced 15%+. FCR improved. Positive agent feedback 70%+.
Phase 3: OptimizeOngoingReview analytics weekly. Tune guardrails. Enable Creator skills. Explore AI Agents for automated resolution. Feed learnings back into data quality improvements.Continuous improvement in metrics. Expanding to more modules and use cases.

Now Assist vs. Other AI Tools — Why Not Just Use ChatGPT?

Now AssistChatGPT / Copilot (External AI)
Data accessReads your incident data, CMDB, KB, and user records directly — no copy-paste neededYou must manually copy data into the AI, risking PII exposure and losing context
ContextKnows the specific record, the related CIs, the assignment group, the SLA statusHas no awareness of your ServiceNow data unless you provide it
IntegrationActions happen inside ServiceNow — generated notes go directly into the field, generated flows deploy immediatelyYou must copy AI output and paste it back into ServiceNow manually
GovernanceGuardrails, audit trails, role-based access, data stays within ServiceNow boundaryNo guardrails — data sent to external servers, no audit trail, potential compliance violations
ComplianceDesigned for enterprise compliance (SOC 2, HIPAA, FedRAMP depending on instance)May violate data handling policies if you paste ticket data into external AI

title: CSDM Explained for Beginners: How Enterprises Connect Business Services to Technology
excerpt: A practical beginner guide to CSDM with examples from banking, retail, and healthcare service mapping.
content:
What is CSDM?

CSDM (Common Service Data Model) is ServiceNow's standard way to model services, applications, technical components, and ownership relationships in CMDB.

In simple terms: CSDM gives one common language so business, operations, and engineering talk about the same service objects.

Why CSDM Matters

  • Incidents can be tied to actual business services.
  • Change risk can be evaluated using service impact context.
  • Executives can see technical outages in business terms.

Enterprise Example: Retail Checkout Outage

Without CSDM, outage records pointed to random servers. Leadership could not assess business impact quickly.

After CSDM alignment, incidents were linked to the Checkout Business Service, enabling instant visibility into affected stores and revenue risk.

CSDM Tables in the Platform

Each CSDM layer maps to a real table you can query:

  • cmdb_ci_service — Business Services (what the business cares about)
  • cmdb_ci_service_auto — Application Services / Service Instances (the deployed app stack that delivers a capability)
  • cmdb_ci_business_app — Business Applications (owned, governed app records)
  • cmdb_ci_appl — Technical Application instances
// Quick CSDM health check: find business apps without owners
var gr = new GlideRecord('cmdb_ci_business_app');
gr.addNullQuery('owned_by'); // Official null API (not addQuery(..., 'NULL'))
gr.addQuery('install_status', '1'); // Installed
gr.query();
var count = 0;
while (gr.next()) { count++; }
gs.info('Unowned business apps: ' + count);

CSDM in Very Simple Layers

LayerWhat it RepresentsExample
Business ServiceWhat the business sells/usesDigital Payments
Application ServiceApp behavior users consumeCheckout API
Application/CITechnical implementationPayment microservice, DB, queue

Most Common Beginner Mistakes

  • Treating every server as a business service.
  • Missing ownership fields (service owner, support group).
  • No relationship governance between app services and CIs.

Start Small

Model 3-5 critical services first (order-to-cash, payroll, identity, customer support) before scaling across the enterprise.

What "Good" Looks Like

  • Incident and change records consistently reference services.
  • Ownership is explicit and complete.
  • Service impact paths are visible in outages and major incidents.

When you are ready for the full picture — every layer, the relationship types, and the GlideRecord queries that trace an outage from a Linux box to a business service — read the deep-dive post "CSDM End to End: How a Single Outage Traces from a Linux Box to a Business Service" on this blog.

title: CMDB for Absolute Beginners: From Asset Lists to Service Impact Intelligence
excerpt: Learn CMDB the easy way with practical enterprise patterns, governance basics, and adoption milestones.
content:
CMDB in One Sentence

CMDB (Configuration Management Database) is the trusted system of record for IT components (CIs) and their relationships.

CMDB vs Asset List

  • Asset list: what you own.
  • CMDB: what exists, how it works, and what depends on what.

Example Scenario: Mobile Banking Latency

An ops team sees database CPU spikes but has no way to tell which customer-facing service is suffering.

With a relationship-aware CMDB, the same alert traces in minutes: DB cluster -> API service -> mobile banking experience.

Key Tables and Tools

In practice, CMDB work centers on a few key areas:

  • cmdb_ci — the base CI table; extended by cmdb_ci_server, cmdb_ci_database, cmdb_ci_appl, etc.
  • CMDB Health Dashboard — tracks completeness, compliance, and duplicate rates across CI classes.
  • Identification and Reconciliation Engine (IRE) — prevents duplicate CIs by matching incoming data against existing records using identification rules.
  • Discovery — auto-populates CMDB by scanning infrastructure (network, compute, storage) and mapping what it finds.

Core CMDB Concepts

  • CI: a managed component (server, app, DB, load balancer).
  • Class: CI type/category.
  • Relationship: dependency path between CIs.
  • Data source: where CI data comes from (discovery, cloud, integrations).

How Enterprises Build CMDB Maturity

  1. Define critical service scope.
  2. Ingest trusted sources first.
  3. Normalize and deduplicate records.
  4. Establish ownership and lifecycle governance.
  5. Use CMDB in incidents/changes/problem workflows.

Common Failure Pattern

Teams load huge CI volumes without governance and call it done. A large CMDB is not useful unless quality and relationships are trusted.

Beginner KPI Set

  • CI completeness
  • Relationship completeness for top services
  • Duplicate CI rate
  • Incidents linked to impacted services

title: ITSM Made Easy: How ServiceNow Standardizes Support at Enterprise Scale
excerpt: A very easy ITSM explainer covering incident, request, problem, and change with practical enterprise examples.
content:
What is ITSM?

ITSM (IT Service Management) is the discipline of delivering and improving IT services using standardized processes.

In ServiceNow, ITSM usually means workflows like Incident, Request, Problem, and Change.

I have seen too many implementations where teams treat ITSM as a ticketing tool and then wonder why operational maturity never improves. The process design matters more than the tool.

The Core Tables

Every ITSM process maps to a real table in the platform:

  • incident — break/fix records
  • sc_request / sc_req_item — service requests and catalog items
  • problem — root cause investigations
  • change_request — planned changes with risk assessment

All four extend the base task table, which means they share common fields like number, state, assigned_to, and priority.

The 4 Building Blocks (Simple View)

PracticeMain GoalTypical Question
IncidentRestore service quickly"How fast can we recover?"
RequestFulfill standard needs"How do we deliver access/device/software?"
ProblemRemove root cause"Why does this keep happening?"
ChangeReduce release risk"How do we change safely?"

Example Scenario: SAP Outage Weekend

Picture how the four practices divide the work after an SAP outage: the incident team restores service fast, the problem team digs into why (a recurring DB patch conflict), and the change team introduces a staged rollout with pre-check gates so the patch cannot break production again.

Outcome: fewer repeat outages and safer monthly release windows.

Why ITSM Programs Fail

  • Tool-first implementation without process ownership.
  • Too many mandatory fields with no operational value.
  • No clear SLAs/OLAs and no queue hygiene.

What Good ITSM Feels Like

  • Users know where to request help.
  • Support teams triage consistently.
  • Changes are assessed for impact and timing.
  • Recurring incidents trigger root-cause work.

Practical Rollout Tip

Start with incident + request standardization, then layer in problem and change maturity once data quality stabilizes.

title: SecOps in ServiceNow: A Beginner-Friendly Guide to Vulnerability Response with Enterprise Examples
excerpt: Understand SecOps in plain language: how vulnerabilities become actionable work, ownership, and measurable reduction.
content:
SecOps in Plain Terms

SecOps in ServiceNow connects security findings with IT remediation workflows so vulnerabilities do not remain as dashboard noise.

Typical Flow

  1. Scanner identifies vulnerability.
  2. Finding is normalized and enriched.
  3. Ownership is assigned to the right team/app.
  4. Remediation tasks are tracked through closure.
  5. Risk posture is reported with evidence.

Beginner-Friendly Terms

  • Finding: scanner output item.
  • Vulnerability item: actionable work record in platform process.
  • Remediation task: assigned action to patch/fix/mitigate.
  • Exception: accepted risk with governance approval.

Key SecOps Tables

TableWhat it stores
sn_vul_entryVulnerability definitions — NVD entries in sn_vul_nvd_entry, third-party scanner entries in sn_vul_third_party_entry
sn_vul_vulnerable_itemCIs affected by a vulnerability
sn_si_incidentSecurity incidents
sn_vul_remediation_taskRemediation work assigned to teams
// Find critical open remediation tasks older than 30 days
var gr = new GlideRecord('sn_vul_remediation_task');
gr.addQuery('state', '!=', 3);  // not closed
gr.addQuery('priority', 1);     // critical
gr.addQuery('sys_created_on', '<', gs.daysAgo(30));
gr.query();
gs.info('Overdue critical remediations: ' + gr.getRowCount());
while (gr.next()) {
    gs.info(gr.getValue('number') + ' | ' +
            gr.getDisplayValue('assigned_to') + ' | ' +
            gr.getDisplayValue('vulnerability'));
}

What Enterprises Measure

  • MTTR for critical vulnerabilities
  • Backlog aging by severity
  • Coverage by business-critical services
  • SLA compliance for remediation

Avoid This Pitfall

Security and operations often use different severity definitions. Align scoring and ownership early to prevent escalation conflicts.

SecOps closes the gap between security findings and actual remediation work. Without it, vulnerability data stays on dashboards. With it, that data turns into accountable work with measurable risk reduction.

title: IRM for Beginners: How ServiceNow Connects Risk, Compliance, and Business Decisions
excerpt: Learn IRM in very simple terms and see how enterprises map controls, risks, and policy evidence in one platform.
content:
What is IRM?

IRM (Integrated Risk Management) helps organizations manage risk, controls, policy obligations, and compliance activities in a connected model.

Instead of siloed spreadsheets, IRM centralizes risk decisions and evidence.

Simple IRM Building Blocks

GRC Tables in the Platform

IRM/GRC ships as scoped applications with their own tables. Two you will meet immediately:

TableWhat it stores
sn_compliance_controlControls — the preventive/detective mechanisms, with owners and attestation state
sn_grc_profileEntities — the things risks and controls apply to (systems, processes, departments)

Policies, risks, issues, and indicators live in further tables within the Policy and Compliance and Risk Management scopes — explore them from the application navigator on a PDI rather than memorizing names.

// Quick look: how many active controls exist? (run in Background Scripts)
var ga = new GlideAggregate('sn_compliance_control');
ga.addQuery('active', true);
ga.addAggregate('COUNT');
ga.query();
if (ga.next()) {
    gs.info('Active controls: ' + ga.getAggregate('COUNT'));
}
  • Risk: what could go wrong and impact objectives.
  • Control: preventive/detective mechanism.
  • Policy/Requirement: governance expectations.
  • Issue: control gap requiring remediation.

Enterprise Example: SOX + ISO Overlap

A global finance organization reduced duplicate audit work by mapping one control to multiple obligations (SOX, ISO, internal policy) and tracking evidence once.

Why Leaders Invest in IRM

  • Single view of enterprise risk posture
  • Clear control ownership
  • Faster audit readiness
  • Fewer manual evidence chases

Beginner Rollout Sequence

  1. Define top enterprise risks and taxonomy.
  2. Map key controls with owners.
  3. Attach obligations and testing schedules.
  4. Track issues and remediation lifecycle.

Keep It Practical

Start with one domain (for example IT risk) and mature operating rhythm before broad enterprise expansion.

title: ServiceNow App Engine Explained: Build Enterprise Apps Without Reinventing the Platform
excerpt: A simple App Engine guide with enterprise examples on workflows, data models, and low-code governance.
content:
What is App Engine?

App Engine is ServiceNow's application development capability for building business apps on the same platform foundation (data, workflow, security, UI, integration).

Why Enterprises Use It

  • Faster delivery vs building every workflow from scratch.
  • Reuse of platform security, approvals, notifications, and reporting.
  • Lower integration and governance overhead.

Example: Vendor Onboarding App

Take a vendor onboarding workflow — risk checks, legal approval, finance sign-off — the kind of process that usually lives in email chains and spreadsheets.

Built with App Engine + Flow Designer, it becomes a trackable, auditable app. The section below sketches exactly that app.

App Engine Core Ingredients

What It Looks Like in Practice

In App Engine Studio, you build an app by defining:

// 1. A custom table (e.g., vendor onboarding requests)
//    Table name: x_myapp_vendor_request
//    Fields: vendor_name (string), status (choice), risk_level (choice),
//            legal_approved (true/false), finance_approved (true/false)

// 2. A Flow Designer flow triggered on record insert:
//    Trigger: Record Created on x_myapp_vendor_request
//    Action 1: Ask for Approval (legal_team group)
//    Action 2: If approved, Ask for Approval (finance_team group)
//    Action 3: If both approved, set status = 'Active'
//    Action 4: Send Notification to requester

// 3. A workspace page (Next Experience UI) for users to submit and track requests

Everything — the table, the flow, the roles, the UI — lives inside a scoped application. You deploy it through Update Sets or Source Control Integration, same as any other ServiceNow customization.

  • Data model (tables/fields)
  • Workflow automation (Flow Designer)
  • Experience/UI components
  • Role-based access control

Beginner Mistakes to Avoid

  • Building app logic before clear process mapping.
  • Ignoring role design and approvals.
  • Creating duplicate tables when standard models already exist.

Governance Matters

Low-code does not mean no architecture. Define app ownership, naming standards, and release controls from day one.
